statement: In 20 adults with cocaine dependence followed through the first three weeks of supervised abstinence on an inpatient research unit (one randomized trial in which half took placebo; this time course is observed across both groups), sleep measured in the sleep laboratory is associated with getting worse while people's own ratings of their sleep improved. From week 1 to week 3, time to fall asleep lengthened (t = -4.9, p < 0.0001), total sleep shortened (t = 2.8, p = 0.008) and REM (dreaming) sleep fell (t = 3.0, p = 0.005), while deep slow-wave sleep rose somewhat (t = -3.5, p = 0.001); over the same weeks, ratings of sleep quality, depth, feeling rested and alertness all improved (for example sleep quality F = 9.0, p = 0.0007). At week 3, people who had taken placebo still had less REM sleep and took longer to fall asleep than 12 healthy men without drug use who were recorded on one night outside the unit, yet rated their sleep at least as good. The authors call this 'occult insomnia' and report the same pattern in an earlier sample of their own (not read here). No group was followed over the same weeks without stopping cocaine or without cocaine dependence, so the unit's fixed routine may also contribute. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In a hospital study of 20 people who had just stopped using cocaine, sleep measured by machines got worse over the first three weeks: falling asleep took longer, total sleep was shorter and dreaming sleep went down, although deep sleep went up a little. At the same time, people felt they were sleeping better and better. By week three, people on a dummy pill still slept worse than healthy men, but did not feel it. It was one small study in a hospital with fixed bedtimes, and nobody was followed outside hospital.
population: Adults with DSM-IV cocaine dependence (mean ages 40 and 44; 16 men, 4 women), mostly seeking treatment, without other psychiatric, sleep or substance dependence disorders apart from nicotine, admitted to an inpatient research unit within days of last use
exposure: Supervised abstinence from cocaine through weeks 1 to 3 after admission (observed time course; half the participants also took modafinil, half placebo)
comparator: The same people's first week of abstinence; at week 3, 12 healthy men without drug use (one laboratory night, not randomized)
outcome: Polysomnographic sleep (time to fall asleep, total sleep, REM and slow-wave sleep) and self-rated sleep quality, depth, feeling rested and alertness
magnitude: Week 1 to week 3, both arms: sleep onset latency longer (t(36) = -4.9, p < 0.0001), total sleep time shorter (t(36) = 2.8, p = 0.008), REM time lower (t(36) = 3.0, p = 0.005), REM latency longer (t(36) = -4.0, p = 0.0003), slow-wave time higher (t(36) = -3.5, p = 0.001); self-rated sleep quality (F(2,36) = 9.0, p = 0.0007), depth (6.3, p = 0.0044), feeling rested (5.9, p = 0.0063) and alertness on waking (8.3, p = 0.0011) improved. Minutes of sleep are shown only in figures. Week 3: three-group differences in total sleep (F(2,29) = 12.1, p < 0.0001), REM time (3.5, p = 0.04), slow-wave time (4.9, p = 0.015) and sleep onset latency (4.7, p = 0.017); self-rated quality 77 (placebo), 81 (modafinil) and 67 (healthy men), p = 0.16.

statement: In 20 adults with cocaine dependence in the first three weeks of supervised inpatient abstinence (one double-blind randomized trial, 10 per group), modafinil, a prescription wake-promoting medicine, compared with placebo, is associated with falling asleep faster (F = 5.8, p = 0.027) and more deep slow-wave sleep (F = 11.9, p = 0.003; more than double the placebo amount) across the three weeks, longer total sleep and an earlier first REM period in week 3, less objective daytime sleepiness in week 1 only (15 against 10 minutes to fall asleep in nap tests) and lower daytime sleepiness ratings at some times of day, but not with better self-rated sleep. More people had side effects on modafinil (6 of 10 against 2 of 10): headache (4 against 1), nausea (2 against 0) and, in one person, palpitations that led to an emergency-department visit. The medicine was given on a schedule fixed by the study team in a hospital unit with set bedtimes, no caffeine and no naps; the study did not test other ways of taking it, effects outside hospital, or whether better sleep helps people stay off cocaine. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In one small hospital trial, people in their first weeks off cocaine who took the prescription medicine modafinil fell asleep faster and had more deep sleep than people on a dummy pill, and by the third week slept longer overall. They did not feel they slept better, and side effects such as headache were more common on modafinil; one person went to an emergency department with a racing heart. The trial was tiny, the medicine was given by doctors on their own schedule, and it did not test whether better sleep helps people stay off cocaine.
population: Adults with DSM-IV cocaine dependence (mean ages 40 and 44; 16 men, 4 women), mostly seeking treatment, without other psychiatric, sleep or substance dependence disorders apart from nicotine, in an inpatient research unit
exposure: Modafinil given by the study team throughout the three study weeks, double-blind (dose and schedule are study conditions in the study card)
outcome: Polysomnographic sleep, daytime sleep latency on nap tests, self-rated sleep and sleepiness, and adverse events
magnitude: Modafinil against placebo: sleep onset latency F(1,18) = 5.8, p = 0.027; slow-wave (N3) time F(1,18) = 11.9, p = 0.0029; week 3 total sleep F(1,36) = 6.7, p = 0.013 and REM latency F(1,36) = 6.9, p = 0.013; REM time not different at any week (p > 0.17); week-1 nap-test sleep latency 15 (SEM 2) against 10 (SEM 2) minutes, F(1,36) = 4.4, p = 0.04; self-rated sleep not different (all p > 0.35); sleepiness ratings drug by week by time-of-day interaction F(4,144) = 2.7, p = 0.036. Adverse events: 6 of 10 against 2 of 10 participants. Minutes of sleep are shown only in figures.

statement: In 30 adults seeking outpatient treatment for heavy cocaine use in New Haven, mostly men in their twenties and thirties who used in binges (14 of them, without other psychiatric diagnoses, described in detail, from their therapists' observations and their own accounts of earlier attempts to stop; Gawin & Kleber, 1986), ending a binge is described as being followed by a crash: low mood mounting within 15 to 30 minutes of the last dose, with intense craving at first that faded if no more cocaine was available; then low mood, loss of pleasure, poor sleep, irritability, anxiety and confusion, ending 1 to 40 hours after use stopped, followed by 8 to 50 hours of heavy sleep with waking and overeating. The paper's figure gives the crash as 9 hours to 4 days, while the text says some people described up to 6 days. During the crash, 43% of the 14 had passing thoughts of suicide and 36% paranoia, both ending with the crash, and over 80% of those described had used sedatives, including alcohol or opioids, at least once to get to sleep. In the later part of the crash people described no craving: five people whose ordered cocaine arrived 2 to 5 hours after their last dose did not use it. A later controlled residential study found mood distress and craving at their highest on admission day, within 48 hours of last use, and falling from then on (Weddington et al., 1990). This is a description of what some people seeking treatment reported, which its authors call preliminary, limited by small numbers and by the lack of structured instruments or blind observation in parts of the study; with no comparison group, it cannot show how often a crash happens, how long it usually lasts, or what causes it. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: People who came for help with heavy cocaine use described a crash after a binge: very low mood and exhaustion, then a long, heavy sleep and a big appetite. It started soon after the last dose and usually ended within a few days. Some had thoughts of suicide or felt paranoid during the crash, and these passed when it ended; many had used alcohol or other drugs to get to sleep. This is what one clinic's patients reported, with no comparison group, so it cannot say how often it happens.
population: Adults seeking outpatient treatment for heavy binge cocaine use (DSM-III cocaine abuse) at one New Haven clinic in the early 1980s; 30 people, 14 described in detail
exposure: The end of a binge of cocaine use (intranasal, smoked or injected; study conditions in the study card)
comparator: None: a clinical description without a comparison group
outcome: Mood, craving, sleep and appetite in the hours and days after a binge (the crash), from clinicians' semistructured interviews and patients' accounts of earlier attempts to stop
magnitude: No rates beyond percentages of the 14 described in detail: passing suicidal thoughts 43%, paranoia 36%, both limited to the crash; over 80% had used alcohol or opioids to sleep. Durations: low mood from 15 to 30 minutes after the last dose, ending 1 to 40 hours after use stopped; heavy sleep 8 to 50 hours; crash 9 hours to 4 days in the figure, up to 6 days in the text.

statement: In 12 men with severe cocaine dependence (10 of them injecting daily) who stopped using in a closed residential research unit in Baltimore, compared with 10 men with no history of drug abuse or dependence living on the same unit (Weddington et al., 1990), the first 28 days without cocaine are associated with mood distress, depression scores and craving that were highest on admission day, within 48 hours of the last use, and lower over the following four weeks, mostly within about two weeks; the authors describe the fall as steady and saw no phases. Self-rated sleep did not differ from the comparison group except more difficulty falling asleep throughout and a larger improvement over time in feeling clear-headed on waking, and both groups slept better over time, which the authors partly put down to getting used to the unit; resting heart rate was lower at first and rose by about 11 beats a minute, and weight gain did not differ. This disagrees with an earlier clinical description, from 30 outpatients' interviews and recollections, of a crash followed by 1 to 10 weeks in which, after a few near-normal days, low pleasure, low energy, anxiety and craving return (Gawin & Kleber, 1986). The settings differ: the residential unit had no cocaine and none of the people, places or objects that set off craving, and the plotted means of several mood scales in the residential study rise again around days 7 to 9 before falling, a pattern its text does not discuss and no test examined. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: Twelve men who stopped cocaine while living in a locked research unit felt worst, and wanted cocaine most, on the day they arrived; over the next four weeks this slowly got better, mostly in the first two weeks. Their sleep was much like that of the 10 men without drug problems living there, except that falling asleep was harder. An older study of people stopping at home described craving coming back after a few calm days. The unit had no cocaine and nothing to remind the men of it, which may explain the difference.

outcome: Self-rated mood (Profile of Mood States, Beck Depression Inventory), craving (cocaine group only), sleep (St Mary's Sleep Questionnaire), heart rate, blood pressure and weight on 11 days

statement: In the samples one review found, a large share of people who use cocaine also used alcohol, and in most samples cannabis, on the same occasions or in the same period, but the share varied widely with the sample and with the definition used. The review combined 16 estimates (11 studies from one PubMed search, January 1990 to June 2017, and 5 of the authors' own analyses of US data sets; 10 from the USA, 3 from Canada, 2 from Brazil and 1 from Denmark; study years 1985 to 2017; samples ranging from household surveys to treatment services, emergency departments, raves and drug courts; all but one by self-report; confidence in the review rated critically low on its study card). Its random-effects averages were 74% (95% CI 50% to 89%) for alcohol and 38% (20% to 60%) for cannabis used on the same occasion as cocaine (the review's definition; the sources asked, for example, about use within a couple of hours, at the first cocaine use, in the same session or to come down from a cocaine high), and 77% (62% to 87%) for alcohol and 64% (47% to 79%) for cannabis used in the same period (from the past 30 days to a lifetime, both positive in one urine test, or an unstated window; where a source gave several windows, the shortest was used), with heterogeneity of 97% to 99% in all four; single sources ranged from about a quarter to nearly all for alcohol and from about 1 in 10 to more than 9 in 10 for cannabis, and the lowest figures came from the narrowest question: in two St Louis samples of women who had used cocaine in the past 30 days, 23.5% and 36.1% said they had used alcohol, and 9.3% and 12.3% cannabis, to come down from cocaine, while 79.5% and 71.3% had drunk alcohol that month. This matters for research on cocaine: of the 40 most recent human brain-imaging studies of cocaine up to January 2018, none excluded people who drink alcohol or use cannabis (two excluded people who had used cannabis in the past week; only 10 excluded alcohol dependence and 10 cannabis dependence, although in most of the studies such dependence was a reason to exclude comparison participants), so unless these drugs were accounted for, their findings may mix effects of cocaine with effects of alcohol or cannabis; of 40 recent animal studies of cocaine, 2 also gave alcohol, both earlier in life (before birth or in adolescence), and none gave cannabis, so those animal studies did not model how people combine these drugs, although the authors note that leaving other drugs out is valid for some questions (Liu et al., 2018). Tobacco, which the authors think may be combined with other drugs, especially alcohol, even more often than cocaine with alcohol, was not counted; the sources were not appraised, the ranges in the text do not all match the review's table, and how many sources entered each average was shown only in a figure that could not be read; an editors' recalculation from the table reproduced two of the four averages (cannabis on the same occasion, alcohol in the same period) but not the other two. What happens in the body when cocaine and alcohol are taken together is in the answer on mixing cocaine and alcohol. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: How often do people who use cocaine also use alcohol or cannabis? Often, in the studies one review found. On average, about 3 in 4 had used alcohol on the same occasion as cocaine or in the same period, and about 4 in 10 had used cannabis on the same occasion, 6 in 10 in the same period. But the numbers varied hugely between groups, from about a quarter to nearly everyone for alcohol and from about 1 in 10 to more than 9 in 10 for cannabis, depending on who was asked and exactly what was asked. This matters for research: none of 40 recent brain-scan studies of cocaine left out people who drink or use cannabis (two left out people who had used cannabis in the past week), so their results may mix up the effects of different drugs, while animal studies almost never gave a second drug. Tobacco was not counted.
population: People who use cocaine in 16 samples (10 US, 3 Canadian, 2 Brazilian, 1 Danish; 1985–2017), from household surveys to treatment services, emergency departments and nightlife settings; and 40 human and 40 animal cocaine studies
exposure: Cocaine use as each source defined it (past 30 days, lifetime, new use, dependence in treatment, emergency-department urine results)
comparator: None for the proportions (one group each); human against animal studies for the research count
outcome: Use of alcohol or cannabis at the same time as cocaine (simultaneous) or in the same period (concurrent), as each source defined it; whether cocaine studies excluded or modelled alcohol and cannabis
magnitude: Liu et al. (2018), random-effects pooled prevalence among people who use cocaine: simultaneous alcohol 74% (95% CI 50–89%), simultaneous cannabis 38% (20–60%), concurrent alcohol 77% (62–87%), concurrent cannabis 64% (47–79%); I² 97–99%; ranges across sources as stated in the text 24–98%, 12–76%, 37–96% and 43–94% (the review's table gives 23.5–87%, 9.3–76.5% and 34.9–96.5% for the first three); number of sources in each estimate not readable (figure not viewable); editors' recalculation from Table 1 (DerSimonian–Laird, logit scale, the review's window and powder rules): simultaneous cannabis 37.9% (19.7–60.3%, 7 sources) and concurrent alcohol 77.0% (62.1–87.2%, 11 sources) reproduce the printed values, simultaneous alcohol 70.1% (46.1–86.5%, 8 sources) and concurrent cannabis 66.5% (49.5–80.1%, 8 sources) do not. St Louis women's samples (n = 463 and 122): alcohol used to come down from cocaine 23.5% and 36.1%, cannabis 9.3% and 12.3%, any past-30-day alcohol 79.5% and 71.3%. Research count: of 40 human cocaine imaging studies, none excluded people who drink or use cannabis (2 excluded cannabis use in the past week), 10 excluded alcohol dependence and 10 cannabis dependence (in most, such dependence excluded comparison participants); of 40 animal cocaine studies, 2 gave alcohol (before birth or in adolescence) and none cannabis; co-use present or modelled in 75% vs 5% (alcohol) and 72.5% vs 0% (cannabis) of human vs animal studies (Fisher's exact p < 0.0001), percentages that measure different things in the two kinds of study.

risk_of_bias.note: Card sc_liu_2018 (AMSTAR 2, critically low): one database, no protocol, no appraisal of the sources, five of the 16 estimates from the authors' own data sets (four from one research programme, two of them women-only and one from drug courts), incompatible definitions and populations pooled; the ranges in the text do not all match the table, and the sources behind each average could not be read (an editors' recalculation from the table reproduces two of the four averages, not the other two).

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: the samples, countries, years and definitions are stated, and no single population is claimed.

imprecision.note: The wide intervals reflect the heterogeneity already rated down; not counted twice.

publication_bias.note: Not assessed by the review; not rated down separately.

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim (proportions in samples): starts low and is never upgraded (METHODS §6.3); down for risk of bias and inconsistency: very low. That a large share of people who use cocaine also used alcohol, and in most samples cannabis, holds in every source the review lists; the averages do not describe any defined population. The count of human and animal studies is the authors' own, and its two percentages measure different things (not excluding people who drink, against giving a second drug); animal studies are counted as designs, not used as evidence about people. Status replicated: the sources are independent samples and all show substantial co-use, though their sizes differ widely.

statement: In New York City in 1993 to 1995, days on which that day's or the previous day's highest temperature reached 31.1 °C (88 °F) (146 of 1,095 days, here called hot days), compared with other days, were associated with more deaths certified by the city's medical examiner as unintentional cocaine overdose: 2.34 a day against 1.76 (341 deaths on hot days, 1,667 on other days), a third more (Marzuk et al., 1998); by the editors' calculation a rate ratio of 1.33 (95% CI 1.18 to 1.49), or about 85 deaths more than the other-day rate predicts, some 4 in 100 of the 2,008 cocaine overdose deaths of those three years. The days were compared without any adjustment for season, day of the week, holidays or trend, and nobody's heat exposure, amount used or pattern of use was known. Deaths from opiates with cocaine absent or present only in clinically insignificant amounts were 0.81 against 0.71 a day and other overdose deaths 0.08 on both kinds of day, neither difference significant, but by the editors' calculation the opiate rate ratio (1.14, 0.93 to 1.38) did not differ significantly from the cocaine one (ratio of the two 1.17, 0.93 to 1.47), so the paper's reading that the rise was specific to cocaine is not established; the share of homicide and traffic victims with cocaine in their blood was much the same on hot and other days (18.9 against 19.5 in 100; 9.5 against 10.3 in 100), which the authors read as cocaine use not rising on hot days; and opiates were also found in about 6 in 10 of the deaths counted as cocaine overdoses. The temperature threshold was chosen from the 1990 to 1992 overdose deaths and the dates of heat deaths with cocaine, then tested on the 1993 to 1995 deaths; the heat-death sampling window was 1990 to 1995 and included those test years, so threshold choice was not demonstrated to be wholly independent of the test period; of 40 tested deaths certified as due to overheating (hyperthermia) in 1990 to 1995, 10 had a breakdown product of cocaine in the body. In a laboratory experiment (Crandall et al., 2002), 7 healthy adults aged 23 to 37 who had never used cocaine were heated at rest in a suit carrying water at 46 °C after one intranasal dose of cocaine (2 mg per kg, described by the authors as low; study conditions) and, on another day in random order, after the same dose of lidocaine, a local anaesthetic used as the comparison (called placebo in the abstract): before heating, core temperature did not differ (36.79 against 36.75 °C), but during heating it rose more after cocaine (P < 0.001; to about 37.79 against 37.55 °C after about 38 minutes, read from the paper's figure and approximate); the skin's blood vessels began to widen, and sweating began, at a core temperature about 0.3 °C higher (37.37 against 37.06 °C and 37.38 against 37.07 °C; by the editors' calculation, 95% CIs of about 0.11 to 0.51 and 0.16 to 0.46 °C); at a core temperature of 37.86 °C, forearm skin vascular conductance (blood-flow signal divided by blood pressure) was 49 against 70 in 100 of its site maximum and sweat rate 0.8 against 1.0 mg per cm² per minute (number contributing is not stated; these are the text values, while Figure 2 has differing plotted endpoints and does not identify whether its significance label concerns an endpoint or the full heating-response comparison); and people felt less hot at the same core temperature. Heat production was not measured, so the authors' conclusion that cocaine raises body temperature mainly by impairing heat loss is an inference; they expect larger doses to add heat production, say the results may not apply to people who use cocaine regularly, and did not test their suggestion that hot weather and crowded clubs amplify the effect. Neither study followed people who used cocaine in hot weather. An editorial published with the New York study (Kilbourne, 1998) said its design shares some features with ecological studies, which are highly open to confounding, and noted that the single hot days compared are not heat waves, so whether heat caused the deaths remains to be established. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: In New York City in the 1990s, hot days had about a third more deaths recorded as cocaine overdoses than other days (2.34 against 1.76 a day). The days were compared without allowing for season or anything else that comes with summer, and the study could not show that the rise happened only with cocaine. In a laboratory, 7 healthy people who had never used cocaine were heated after one small dose: their skin began to flush and sweat only at a higher body temperature, their body temperature rose more than after a comparison drug, and they felt less hot. Neither study looked at people using cocaine in hot weather.
population: Deaths certified by the New York City medical examiner in 1993 to 1995 (2,008 unintentional cocaine overdose deaths; 793 opiate and 85 other overdose deaths as comparisons; threshold chosen on 1990 to 1992 deaths); 7 healthy adults aged 23 to 37 who had never used cocaine, in a laboratory in Dallas
exposure: Hot days (that day's or the previous day's maximum temperature at least 31.1 °C, 88 °F, in Central Park); in the laboratory, one intranasal dose of cocaine hydrochloride (2 mg per kg) before passive whole-body heating at rest (study conditions)
comparator: Other days; in the laboratory, the same people after the same dose of lidocaine, an active local anaesthetic control
outcome: Daily number of deaths certified as unintentional cocaine overdose (opiate and other overdose deaths, and cocaine in the blood of homicide and traffic victims, as comparisons); core temperature, skin blood flow, sweating and how hot people felt during heating
magnitude: Marzuk et al. (1998), New York City 1993–1995: cocaine overdose deaths 2.34 a day (SD 1.68; 341 deaths on 146 hot days) against 1.76 (SD 1.37; 1,667 on 949 other days), Mann-Whitney z = 3.98, P < .001, 33% higher mean; opiate overdose deaths with cocaine absent or clinically insignificant 0.81 (SD 0.94) against 0.71 (SD 0.86), P = .28; other overdose deaths 0.08 against 0.08, P = .69; cocaine in blood of homicide victims 18.9% (136/719) against 19.5% (766/3,919), of traffic victims aged 15–54 9.5% (12/126) against 10.3% (71/689); opiates in 57.1% and 61.7% of cocaine overdose deaths (hot, other days); deaths certified as hyperthermia 1990–1995: benzoylecgonine in 10 of 40 tested (21% of all 48). Editors' calculations (Poisson, ignoring overdispersion and the reported autocorrelation of 0.12, so somewhat too narrow): cocaine rate ratio 1.33 (1.18 to 1.49); opiates 1.14 (0.93 to 1.38); ratio of the two 1.17 (0.93 to 1.47); about 85 excess deaths, about 4% of 2,008. Crandall et al. (2002), 7 cocaine-naive adults, cocaine against lidocaine, mean ± SE: core temperature before heating 36.79 ± 0.01 against 36.75 ± 0.08 °C; greater rise during heating, P < 0.001 (about 37.79 against 37.55 °C after about 38 min, read from Figure 1, approximate); onset of skin vasodilation at 37.37 ± 0.09 against 37.06 ± 0.07 °C (P = 0.01) and of sweating at 37.38 ± 0.09 against 37.07 ± 0.06 °C (P = 0.002), slopes unchanged; at 37.86 °C, skin vascular conductance 49 ± 9 against 70 ± 5% of maximum (P = 0.03) and sweat rate 0.8 ± 0.2 against 1.0 ± 0.1 mg/cm² per minute (P = 0.04), number contributing not stated; Figure 2 has differing plotted endpoints and does not identify the endpoint or full-response model term behind its significance label, so no reconciled endpoint analysis is inferred; before heating, mean arterial pressure 93 ± 3 against 85 ± 3 mm Hg and heart rate 74 ± 5 against 67 ± 4 beats/min. Editors' calculation from the rounded P values: threshold shifts of 0.31 °C (95% CI about 0.11 to 0.51 and 0.16 to 0.46 °C).

risk_of_bias.note: Day comparison (card sc_marzuk_1998): ROBINS-E high, entirely unadjusted (season, day of week, holidays and trend not modelled); deaths counted through the medical examiner's certification; the negative-control comparisons are imprecise and were not compared with the cocaine estimate. Laboratory study (card sc_crandall_2002): RoB 2 some concerns (how the order was randomized not reported; blinding not checked although cocaine raised heart rate and blood pressure, which matters for the felt heat; number contributing at the highest temperatures unknown; no protocol; about 22 comparisons without correction).

inconsistency.note: The two studies answer different parts of the question (deaths on hot days; heat-loss responses in the laboratory), and no replication of either was read.

indirectness.note: One city in 1993 to 1995 and counts of deaths per day, not anyone's own heat exposure or use; the laboratory study gave one low intranasal dose to 7 people who had never used cocaine, heated passively at rest, unlike use outside the laboratory (larger or repeated amounts, exertion, other drugs).

imprecision.note: Seven people in the laboratory, with the intervals for the comparisons at 37.86 °C close to no difference; the opiate comparison cannot exclude a rise of about a third. The cocaine rate ratio itself is precise (1.18 to 1.49).

large_effect.note: Not applied: a rate ratio of 1.33 from an unadjusted comparison.

dose_response.note: Not applied: the paper's 'steady increase' above the threshold rests on cumulative and moving-average curves without a test of trend (card reporting issues).

grade.reasoning: The day comparison is observational and starts low; rated down for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision, it is very low. The laboratory study, rated alone, would start high as a randomized crossover and be rated down for risk of bias, indirectness (one low dose in people who had never used cocaine, at rest) and imprecision (7 people), also very low. 'Is associated with': the death counts come from an unadjusted comparison of days, and the laboratory study shows what one dose did to heat-loss responses under passive heating, not what happens to people who use cocaine in hot weather. Status single study: each part rests on one study; the laboratory study is consistent with the death counts but does not replicate them, and it takes them as its starting point. The editorial published with the New York study (Kilbourne, 1998) has now been read and is cited for its appraisal, which changes no rating. Not read: the published letter on the laboratory study with the authors' reply (Schier et al., 2002), a later study of the same association (Auger et al., 2017) and population studies of heat and drug deaths on the reading list. The post-mortem cocaine levels that the laboratory paper's introduction cites are second-hand and not used.

statement: In six people who smoked cocaine almost daily, living on an inpatient research unit, cocaine was chosen over a $5 voucher on most occasions but not all: the voucher was taken more often when the cocaine dose was smaller, and slightly more often when it was for cash than when it was for goods, a difference that cannot be separated from the order of the sessions; with no session offering cocaine without an alternative, the study cannot show how much the vouchers lowered cocaine taking. The four women and two men (aged 30 to 39, recruited in New York City by word of mouth and newspaper advertisements, spending $100 to $500 a week on cocaine; whether they wanted treatment is not stated) each completed eight sessions; in each, after a sample trial, they chose five times, 14 minutes apart, between one dose of smoked cocaine (study conditions: 0, a dummy dose, or 12, 25 or 50 mg, one dose level per session) and a voucher that could be exchanged at discharge for $5 in cash or for $5 of goods, each choice requiring 200 key presses, and the four money-voucher sessions always came before the four merchandise-voucher sessions. Cocaine choices rose with dose (F(3, 15) = 15.26, P < 0.001) and were fewer with the money voucher (F(1, 5) = 7.48, P < 0.05), with no significant difference at any single dose. On the editors' reading of the figures, cocaine was chosen on average 10.7 of 20 times with the money voucher and 12.8 with the merchandise voucher (difference 2.2 choices, 95% CI 0.1 to 4.2, editors' calculation), more than a third of the difference coming from the dummy-dose sessions; with active doses, cocaine was chosen on 60 and 68 of 90 occasions (about 2 in 3 and 3 in 4), at 12 mg about half the time (2.5 and 2.7 of 5) and at 50 mg about 3 times in 4 with the money voucher and 9 in 10 with the merchandise voucher (3.8 and 4.5 of 5) (Hart et al., 2000). The study measured choices in a laboratory, between an immediate dose and a small reward that could be used only at discharge, not cocaine use outside it; the authors judged order effects unlikely, from their other studies and because all participants reported using much more cocaine outside the laboratory than in the sessions; the authors' extension to treatment that rewards drug-free tests with vouchers (contingency management) was not tested here; and the earlier laboratory studies they cite, in which larger money alternatives lowered cocaine choice, were not read. Rat studies of choices between cocaine and other rewards are in the answer on the Rat Park studies. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Do people choose other rewards over cocaine when they can? Sometimes. In a lab study, six people who smoked cocaine almost daily chose, many times, between a dose of cocaine and a $5 voucher. With real doses they took the voucher about 1 time in 3 or 4: about half the time at the smallest dose, and less often at the largest. The vouchers could only be cashed or spent when they left the hospital. They took a cash voucher a little more often than a voucher for goods, but the cash sessions always came first, so the order may explain it. The study was tiny, measured choices in a lab rather than use in daily life, and never offered cocaine without another choice.
population: Six adults who smoked cocaine almost daily (four women, two men; aged 30–39; recruited in New York City; whether they sought treatment is not stated), living on an inpatient research unit
exposure: Repeated choices between one dose of smoked cocaine (study conditions: 0, 12, 25 or 50 mg; one dose level per session) and a $5 voucher for cash (sessions 1–4) or for goods (sessions 5–8), redeemable only at discharge
comparator: The same participants with the other kind of voucher, and at other dose levels; no session without an alternative
outcome: Number of cocaine choices out of five per session (out of 20 per kind of voucher)
magnitude: Dose F(3, 15) = 15.26, P < 0.001; kind of voucher F(1, 5) = 7.48, P < 0.05; no significant voucher difference at any single dose. Editors' reading of Figure 2 (totals of 20, money vs merchandise): 15 vs 16, 7 vs 7, 12 vs 14, 12 vs 16, 2 vs 7, 16 vs 17; means 10.7 vs 12.8; mean paired difference 2.17 (95% CI 0.13 to 4.20; dz 1.12; editors' calculation, reproducing the printed F). Editors' reading of Figure 1 (mean choices of 5, money vs merchandise): 0 mg 0.67 vs 1.50; 12 mg 2.50 vs 2.67; 25 mg 3.67 vs 4.17; 50 mg 3.83 vs 4.50; active doses 60 vs 68 of 90 choices; 0.83 of the 2.17 difference (38%) from the dummy-dose sessions; at 50 mg, 77% and 90% of choices (editors' calculation). Vouchers redeemable only at discharge.

risk_of_bias.note: The money sessions always came first, so the kind of voucher cannot be separated from time on the unit; participants knew which voucher was on offer although the study is called double-blind; subjective, heart-rate, blood-pressure and blood measures were collected but not reported (card sc_hart_2000: RoB 2 high; because the voucher order was fixed, the protocol's instrument for this comparison would be ROBINS-I, a question left to the senior author, and the overall judgment is at the most severe level either way).

indirectness.note: Six inpatients not described as seeking treatment, choosing between single smoked doses and $5 vouchers usable only at discharge, five times a session in a laboratory; choices, not use or abstinence outside it.

imprecision.note: Six participants; the voucher difference (about 2 of 20 choices, 95% CI 0.1 to 4.2, editors' calculation) rests on one F test at P < 0.05, and no single dose showed a difference.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for a single study.

grade.reasoning: A within-person laboratory study, but the conditions were not randomized or counterbalanced (money sessions first; the order of doses not reported), so it starts low (METHODS 6.3). Down one each for risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision, which is below the floor: very low. The statement keeps to what the choices show: that people who smoked cocaine frequently chose a small non-drug reward on part of the occasions, more often at smaller doses. Whether alternatives reduce cocaine use, and the authors' extension to contingency management, are not claimed. Figure values are the first reader's readings at 300 dpi (bar heights on whole numbers, reproducing the printed F by a paired t), labelled as the editors' readings and calculations. The verb is 'is associated with' because the kind of voucher coincides with the order of sessions. No replication of the cash-against-goods comparison was read. A related answer on methamphetamine describes choices between methamphetamine and money.

statement: In laboratory studies of men who already used cocaine often, smoked and injected cocaine reached the blood within seconds, and the effects they rated peaked within about 1 to 1.5 minutes and had mostly faded within 15 to 30 minutes, while cocaine was still in the blood at 90 minutes; the snorted route was not measured in the studies read. In 9 men on a residential research unit who used both injected and smoked cocaine (study conditions, not amounts to use: 16 or 32 mg injected and 25 or 50 mg smoked, each given over 15 seconds, with each route's doses in rising order about 90 minutes apart), arterial levels peaked about 15 seconds after the dose ended, at roughly ten times the later arm-vein peak (at that moment, after 32 mg injected, 2347 ng/ml in arterial against 27 ng/ml in arm-vein blood), while arm-vein levels peaked at about 4 minutes; the two approached each other within about 20 minutes, and at 90 minutes levels after the higher doses were still above those after the lower ones. Ratings of feeling stimulated, high and liking the drug peaked about 1.0 to 1.5 minutes after either route, stayed raised for about 10 minutes, were low by 15 to 30 minutes and were no longer reported at 90 minutes; blood pressure and heart rate (about 107 beats a minute after the highest doses) peaked within about 1 to 1.5 minutes. Smoked doses gave lower blood levels than injected doses (arm-vein peaks 67 and 143 against 108 and 252 ng/ml), yet peak ratings and peak systolic pressure did not differ significantly between routes; because sham smoking itself raised blood pressure and ratings of high, and no effect was compared with placebo or sham, the study cannot show that one route gives a stronger effect for the same blood level. Of 13 men who started, 4 were discharged in the first phase, 3 for transient premature ventricular contractions (extra heartbeats; 2 of them had received only placebo injections) and 1 for chest pain after a single smoked dose, so the men analysed are those who tolerated every dose (Evans et al., 1996). In 4 men given 100 or 200 mg into a vein over 1.5 to 3 minutes after at least 48 hours without cocaine, the highest measured level was in the first arm sample, at 5 minutes, and its terminal half-life, the time the level took to halve in the later hours, was 40 to 52 minutes after 100 mg and 79 to 82 minutes after 200 mg; the paper's equations relating half-life to dose rest on five sessions with doses compared mostly between different men, and its early values lie above the assay's calibrated range (Barnett et al., 1981). For snorting, the same paper's figures of about 60% absorbed and an 8-minute absorption half-life come from refitting another laboratory's averaged curves, which peaked between 20 and 60 minutes and were sampled only to 90 minutes; the authors call the absorption estimates imprecise. A 1996 narrative review describes, second-hand from studies not read here, peak levels in venous blood about 30 to 40 minutes after snorting against about 5 minutes after injecting or smoking, peak felt effects within 10 to 20 minutes after snorting and effects lasting about 60 minutes or longer after that peak (against about 30 to 45 minutes in all after injecting or smoking, a duration counted differently), and a share absorbed after snorting that ranged from 25% to 94% across studies (Hatsukami & Fischman, 1996). None of the studies read tested what happens when people take more because they feel little at first. Both primary studies were small, gave doses in an order that was not randomized and studied only men who used cocaine often. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: How fast does cocaine work, and how long does it last? In a laboratory study of 9 men who often smoked and injected cocaine, smoked or injected cocaine reached the blood within seconds. The high, and a faster heartbeat and higher blood pressure, peaked after about 1 to 1.5 minutes, and the high was mostly gone within 15 to 30 minutes, although cocaine was still in the blood at 90 minutes. In another small study of 4 men, the amount of cocaine in the blood halved about every 40 to 80 minutes in the later hours after an injection, more slowly in the two sessions with the bigger dose. Snorting was not measured in these studies: an older review says, from studies we have not read, that snorted cocaine takes longer to reach its peak and lasts longer, so the high comes on more slowly. None of these studies tested what happens when people then take more. These were small studies of men who used cocaine often, given set doses in a laboratory.
population: Men who used cocaine often, studied in laboratories: 9 men who used both injected and smoked cocaine, on a residential research unit (Evans et al., 1996); 4 men with frequent use given injected cocaine (Barnett et al., 1981); snorting only through a reanalysis of another laboratory's averaged data and a 1996 narrative review
exposure: Cocaine given by the researchers: injected (cocaine hydrochloride) or smoked (cocaine base), at each study's doses and timing; study conditions only
comparator: Arterial against arm-vein blood drawn at the same moments; injected against smoked cocaine in the same men; lower against higher doses (placebo and sham sessions were run but not analysed)
outcome: Time course of blood cocaine levels, heart rate, blood pressure and rated effects (stimulated, high, drug liking); elimination half-life
magnitude: Evans et al. (1996), 8 to 9 men, 15-second administration: arterial peak about 15 seconds after the end of administration (after 32 mg injected, 2347 ng/ml arterial against 27 ng/ml arm-vein at that moment); arm-vein peaks at about 4 minutes, 108 and 252 ng/ml after 16 and 32 mg injected and 67 and 143 ng/ml after 25 and 50 mg smoked; arterial peaks higher, F(1,7) = 91.353, P < .0001, and earlier, F(1,7) = 52.158, P < .0002, than arm-vein peaks, with no difference in timing by route or dose; injected above smoked peaks, F(1,7) = 7.613, P < .0281. Ratings peaked at about 1.0 (high), 1.25 (liking) and 1.5 minutes (stimulated), stayed raised about 10 minutes, were low by 15 to 30 minutes and absent at 90 minutes (data not shown); heart rate peaked near 107 beats a minute at 1.45 minutes on average; systolic pressure at the first reading, about 1 minute (cuff peaks 158 and 154 mm Hg after 32 mg injected and 50 mg smoked). Barnett et al. (1981), 4 men, 100 or 200 mg into a vein over 1.5 to 3 minutes: 5-minute levels 682 to 1005 ng/ml after 100 mg and 2530 and 3868 ng/ml after 200 mg, the highest measured in each session; terminal half-lives 40.3, 47.2 and 51.5 minutes after 100 mg and 78.9 and 82.3 minutes after 200 mg (51.5 against 82.3 in the one man given both). Snorting, not measured in either study: about 60% absorbed and an absorption half-life of 8.4 minutes (coefficient of variation of the rate constant 72%), from a refit of another laboratory's averaged curves whose observed peak lay between 20 and 60 minutes (Barnett et al., 1981); venous peak about 30 to 40 minutes, peak felt effects within 10 to 20 minutes and effects lasting about 60 minutes or longer after that peak, with 25% to 94% absorbed across studies, as described second-hand by a narrative review (Hatsukami & Fischman, 1996). No interval is given for any time estimate.

evidence.extracted: Study conditions: 13 men with current use of both injected and smoked cocaine started and 9 completed (7 African-American and 2 Caucasian; mean age 34, range 24–45; both routes for an average of 7.5 years, each at least two or three times a week, about 2.5 g a week; all used other drugs). Both routes were given over 15 seconds: cocaine hydrochloride 0, 8, 16 or 32 mg injected (10-second injection plus 5-second flush) and cocaine base sham, 12.5, 25 or 50 mg smoked from a pipe in one staff-timed administration. Four men were medically discharged during phase I: 3 for transient premature ventricular contractions (two of whom had received only intravenous placebo) and 1 for chest pain after a single 25 mg smoked dose.

risk_of_bias.note: Both studies are at high risk on their study cards (RoB 2): the order of doses was not randomized (Evans et al.: rising doses within a day and the order of the two test days not reported; Barnett et al.: doses compared mostly between different men), the route was open, ratings were spoken aloud to staff, the smoked dose actually inhaled is unknown, and Barnett et al.'s early values lie above the assay's calibrated range. The arterial against arm-vein comparison, on samples drawn at the same moments, is the least biased part.

inconsistency.note: The two studies measured different things; where they overlap (the highest arm-vein level within about 5 minutes of an injected dose) they agree.

indirectness.note: Men only, experienced with both routes or using often; a timed 15-second smoking procedure unlike usual smoking and injections over 15 seconds to 3 minutes; laboratory doses; snorting, the most common route, only through a reanalysis of another laboratory's averaged data and a narrative review.

imprecision.note: 8 to 9 and 4 men; no interval for any time estimate; half-lives from five sessions.

grade.reasoning: Descriptive laboratory timing data start low (relation 'describes', METHODS §6.1, §6.3). Risk of bias −1, indirectness −1 and imprecision −1 take the rating below the floor: very low. Status single study: each finding rests on one primary study (Evans et al., 1996, for the timing of effects and of arterial against arm-vein levels by route; Barnett et al., 1981, for elimination after injected doses), which agree only on the early arm-vein peak after injection; the narrative review's figures for snorting are second-hand and used only to qualify. Not used, following the study cards: Barnett et al.'s general equations relating half-life and clearance to dose (five sessions, mostly between different men), its threshold in initial concentration (it mixes fitted model types) and its build-up after a repeated dose (one session in one man, outside the methods and above the calibrated range); Evans et al.'s conclusion that smoked cocaine does not reach the brain faster than injected cocaine (brain levels were not measured, and arterial samples were 15 seconds apart).

verification.flag_note: Snorting, the route most people use, is not measured in any primary study read; a laboratory study of intranasal cocaine (for example Javaid et al., 1978, or Jeffcoat et al., 1989, cited by these papers) should be read before the page gives timings for snorted cocaine on primary evidence.

statement: Crack and powder are the same drug in two forms. A 1996 narrative review puts most differences between them down to the route each form allows and the speed and amount of cocaine it delivers, and to the amounts people use, rather than to the form itself; a 2017 systematic review names crack's own pharmacology and routes, and the marginalized circumstances of many people who use it, as possible explanations without testing them. No source read tests crack against powder with route, amount and circumstances accounted for. Powder cannot be smoked because it breaks down at the temperature needed to vaporize it, while the base form (crack) can, so to some extent the form sets the route: crack is smoked, powder is snorted or injected. Once in the blood, the 1996 review describes the two forms as eliminated and broken down alike, with peak levels in venous blood about 5 minutes after smoking or injecting against about 30 to 40 minutes after snorting (second-hand from studies not read here; Hatsukami & Fischman, 1996). In US household surveys of 1995–1998, among 762 people who had started cocaine within roughly the previous 0–23 months, each of seven dependence features was reported more often by the 190 who had started crack (some of whom had also just started powder) than by the 572 who had started powder and never used crack: weighted occurrence in the past year about 18% to 32% against about 5% to 12%, or about 2.5 to 4.4 times as often by the editors' reading of the figure. The summary odds ratio across features, adjusted for sex, age, race, daily drinking, daily tobacco smoking, injecting and the number of days cocaine was used, was 1.9 (95% CI 1.4 to 2.5), and 1.6 (1.0 to 2.5) for a further 93 people who had recently started crack after two or more years of powder use; without the term for days of use the estimate was about 2.3 to 3.7, reported without intervals (Chen & Anthony, 2004). Those estimates come from one interview, with use, form and problems all self-reported and no measure of how people differed before they started; the authors say a greater susceptibility among people who start crack cannot be ruled out, and they fitted the model with and without days of use because dependence itself may raise use, so adjusting for it may remove part of a real difference. The 2017 systematic review of 302 included articles pooled only comparisons of crack use against people not using drugs or the general population, never against powder. In its narrative synthesis, comparisons of people using crack with people using other forms of cocaine were described as mixed for anxiety disorders, dependence on alcohol, cocaine or other substances, and depression (12 studies), and as showing no difference for 10 other diagnoses (5 studies); single studies found more anorexia and insomnia and less suicidal thinking with crack, and more violence toward others than among people snorting cocaine but not more than among people injecting it; the review neither pooled nor tested these comparisons. Its authors judge crack not a plausible direct cause of the infections and violence linked with its use, reading crack use as a facilitator or marker of risk behaviours and risk environments, and call it unclear for mental health whether crack use is a cause, a consequence or comorbid (Butler et al., 2017). The 1996 review, whose evidence on patterns of use comes from uncontrolled surveys and treatment, street and jail samples, mostly of the mid-1980s to early 1990s, reports that people who smoke or inject cocaine typically use it more often and in larger amounts than people who snort it (one Miami sample found the largest amounts among people snorting), that people who smoke crack reach regular use sooner than people who snort or inject, and that smoking or injecting goes with a faster onset of problems and earlier treatment; its statement that differences disappear once the amount used is held constant rests partly on two sets of meeting proceedings published before crack appeared. No comparison of crack with powder in the sources read adjusts for the amount taken per occasion, for illegal drugs other than cocaine, or for income, housing or the policing people met; the household survey adjusts for daily drinking, daily smoking, injecting and days of use. Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: Does crack lead to dependence more often, or do more harm, than powder cocaine? They are the same drug in two forms. Powder cannot be smoked, so to some extent the form sets how people take it: smoked or injected cocaine peaks in the blood within minutes, while snorted cocaine peaks after about half an hour. In US surveys from 1995 to 1998 of people who had just started cocaine, about 18 to 32 in 100 of those who had started crack reported each sign of dependence, against about 5 to 12 in 100 of those who used only powder; after allowing for how many days they had used and a few other things, the difference was smaller but still there. These surveys asked people once, so they cannot show that crack itself is the reason: people who start crack may differ to begin with, and they tend to use more. A later review of 302 studies found comparisons between crack and other forms of cocaine mixed; its authors say crack is not a likely direct cause of the infections and violence linked to it, and that for mental health the reasons are unclear.
population: People in US households, 1995–1998 surveys: 762 who had started cocaine within roughly the previous 0–23 months (572 powder only; 190 recent crack, some of whom had also just started powder) and 93 who had recently started crack after two or more years of powder use; the samples of a 2017 systematic review of 302 included articles on crack use, mostly marginalized high-risk groups in the USA, Brazil and Canada; the treatment, survey, laboratory and administrative sources of a 1996 narrative review
exposure: Crack (smoked cocaine base), compared with cocaine hydrochloride powder (snorted or injected)
comparator: People who had started powder cocaine and never used crack; in the 2017 review's pooled estimates, people not using drugs or the general population (crack against other forms of cocaine only in its narrative synthesis)
outcome: Dependence features, mental-health and other health outcomes, and patterns of use
magnitude: Chen & Anthony (2004), weighted past-year occurrence of seven dependence features: about 5% to 12% among 572 people who had started powder only; about 18% to 32% among 190 who had recently started crack and about 11% to 33% among 93 who had started crack after two or more years of powder use (the group ranges are the first reader's readings of a figure that prints no values). Unadjusted odds ratios, recent crack against powder only: reduced activities 5.6 (1.9 to 15.9), tolerance 4.8 (1.8 to 12.6), inability to cut down 4.0 (1.9 to 8.7), emotional problems 3.5 (1.6 to 7.7), salience 3.4 (1.5 to 7.7), using more than intended 3.1 (1.4 to 7.0), health problems 3.0 (0.9 to 9.7). Adjusted summary across the seven features: 1.9 (1.4 to 2.5) for recent crack and 1.6 (1.0 to 2.5) for crack after two or more years of powder; about 2.3 to 3.7 without the days-of-use term (no intervals). These are odds ratios although the paper calls them relative risks; from the figure the corresponding prevalence ratios are about 2.5 to 4.4 for recent crack and about 1.5 to 3.3 for crack after powder (editors' calculation from the figure readings). Butler et al. (2017): no pooled crack-versus-powder estimate; 12 studies mixed and 5 showing no difference, none pooled or tested by the review; one study found more violence toward others with crack than with snorted cocaine, and no difference from injected cocaine. Hatsukami & Fischman (1996), second-hand: two thirds of people smoking crack used daily against 18% of people snorting powder, among people interviewed in treatment, street, jail or prison settings in New York City in 1988–1989; in the 1991 national survey, crack use was 52.5% among people who used cocaine frequently and 17.5% among those who used it infrequently (neither defined), injecting 24.3% against 9.3%.

risk_of_bias.note: ROBINS-E high on the study card for the survey comparison: one cross-sectional interview, self-reported form, use and problems, no measure of how people differed before starting, and adjustment that cannot separate the form from the amount used (days of use may itself be a consequence of dependence). The 1996 review is a narrative review whose sources are unappraised (editors' checklist: high), and the 2017 systematic review is AMSTAR 2 critically low and pools nothing for this comparison.

inconsistency.note: The household survey finds a consistent excess across all seven features, while the 2017 review describes the crack-versus-other-cocaine literature on dependence, anxiety and depression as mixed and lists 10 diagnoses with no difference.

indirectness.note: Second-hand for much of it: the pharmacology and the patterns of use come through a narrative review of studies not read here, and the 2017 review's pooled estimates compare crack with people not using drugs or the general population rather than with powder. The survey evidence is from 1995–1998 and DSM-IV items, and no source adjusts for the amount taken per occasion together with illegal drugs other than cocaine, income, housing or policing.

imprecision.note: The adjusted survey estimates have usable intervals (1.4 to 2.5; 1.0 to 2.5), and the claim does not rest on the wide unadjusted feature-level estimates.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for the narrative review; the 2017 review examined funnel plots for other outcomes, not for this comparison.

large_effect.note: Not applied: the estimate stays above 2 only without the term for days of use, and the remaining confounding (susceptibility before onset, amount used) runs away from the null (METHODS §6.3).

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low. Risk of bias −1, inconsistency −1 and indirectness −1 take it below the floor: very low. The claim is worded as an association and is rated as one (METHODS §6.3). Status mixed: a population survey finds an excess of dependence features with crack that shrinks after adjustment, while the one systematic review covering the same question describes the comparisons as mixed and pools none, and the 1996 review attributes the differences to route, amount and context without testing them. The three sources are not independent: the 2017 review includes Chen & Anthony (2004) in its narrative synthesis and cites the 1996 review as background, so they are counted once. Not used, following the study cards: a causal effect of smoking crack, the 1996 review's figures as measurements, its gateway reading of sequence data, and any crack-versus-powder difference in physical harms, for which the sources read give only second-hand, unadjusted figures.

verification.flag_note: The three sources overlap (the 2017 review covers Chen & Anthony, 2004, and cites the 1996 review), so they are counted once for replication. The sentencing and criminal-justice material in the 1996 review, and the 2017 review's findings on infections, maternal outcomes and violence, are outside this question and belong to other claims. No source read compares crack with powder holding the amount used constant; a study that does would change this answer.

statement: In US household surveys from 2002 to 2016 (National Surveys on Drug Use and Health), among people who had first used cocaine less than 12 months before the interview, an estimated 5.0% (95% CI 4.0% to 6.3%) of those who had used only powder, and 22.2% (16.7% to 29.4%) of those who had gone on to crack, met DSM-IV criteria for cocaine dependence by the time they were interviewed; the estimates are summaries of seven two-year survey pairs (2014 is not among them), based on the paper's unweighted totals of 3,488 powder-only and 275 powder-then-crack initiates, which its Methods describe as effective sample sizes back-calculated from the survey output (9 to 96 per year-pair in the second group). Of 21 dependence-related problems asked about, the most frequent in both groups was wanting or trying to cut down or stop using cocaine (45.4%, 43.1% to 47.9%, against 58.3%, 53.0% to 64.2%) and the least frequent was continuing to use despite physical problems caused or worsened by cocaine (1.9% against 2.8%, the difference not significant); most of the other problems were more common in the group who had gone on to crack, with at least one exception and one item whose estimate the paper does not plot. The two groups are not comparable exposures: the comparison is unadjusted, the survey asks about cocaine in any form rather than which form caused a problem, and reaching crack within the same 12 months takes time and continued use, so time since first use, which is not reported for either group, and amount used may differ. The paper's authors give three readings of the difference without choosing between them: people who go on to crack may be more susceptible from the outset; some may become dependent on powder and then start crack; or something about crack smoking may raise the risk. Dependence was scored against DSM-IV criteria from people's own answers in a computer interview, in a household and group-quarters survey (people in institutions are outside the sampling frame), without characteristics reported for either group, and the item wording sits in supplements that were not available. The 22% is not shown to be the same as the roughly 30% reported for newly started heroin use in a separate study: no test is reported and the interval stops at 29.4%. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: How quickly can dependence start after someone first uses cocaine? In US surveys, about 5 in 100 people who had started cocaine in the past year, and used only powder, met the criteria for cocaine dependence by the time they were asked. Among those who had also gone on to crack, it was about 22 in 100. The most common problem in both groups was wanting or trying to cut down or stop. This does not show that crack itself causes dependence: people who go on to crack may differ to begin with, some may already have problems with powder, and the survey did not ask which form caused a problem. The surveys relied on what people said about themselves, and most people who start cocaine do not meet the criteria within the first year.
population: People aged 12 and over in US households and non-institutional group quarters who had first used cocaine less than 12 months before interview, 2002–2016 National Surveys on Drug Use and Health (seven two-year pairs; 2014 not included): 3,488 powder-only and 275 powder-then-crack initiates in all (effective sample sizes per two-year pair 194–590 and 9–96)
exposure: Having first used cocaine within the past 12 months: powder only, or powder followed by crack (self-reported)
comparator: People who had started powder cocaine and never used crack (unadjusted comparison)
outcome: Meeting DSM-IV criteria for cocaine dependence, and 21 dependence-related problems, by the time of interview
magnitude: Chandra & Anthony (2020), meta-analysis summaries of seven two-year survey pairs: dependence within 1–12 months of first use 5.0% (95% CI 4.0% to 6.3%) in powder-only initiates and 22.2% (16.7% to 29.4%) in powder-then-crack initiates (the paper's Conclusions print 20% for the second). Year-pair estimates 2.9% to 7.0% and 10.3% to 30.0%, the widest interval running from 9.2% to 64.5%. Problem items: wanting or trying to cut down or stop 45.4% (43.1% to 47.9%) against 58.3% (53.0% to 64.2%), difference p < 0.05; continuing to use despite physical problems 1.9% (1.6% to 2.4%) against 2.8% (1.6% to 5.2%), p > 0.05. The study card's reading of the figure: powder-only estimates below 10% for 17 of the 20 plotted items, powder-then-crack estimates 15% or more for 14; one item about equal in the two groups and one (about 36% against 28%) higher in the powder-only group. No adjusted estimate, no absolute difference with an interval and no per-month risk are given.

risk_of_bias.note: JBI prevalence appraisal on the study card: moderate risk. Dependence is derived by algorithm from self-report items whose wording was not available; no characteristics of either group are reported; time since first use, which ranges up to 12 months and may differ between the groups, is not reported; non-response handling is not described; the comparison between the two groups is unadjusted and, as the authors say, confounded by susceptibility before onset and by the reverse sequence.

inconsistency.note: Powder-only year-pair estimates (2.9% to 7.0%) differ by more than chance alone would explain (editors' reconstruction from the year-pair values in Fig. 1, recomputed in adjudication: I-squared about 58%), while the powder-then-crack estimates (10.3% to 30.0%) vary within what their small samples allow; the paper's stated rule for choosing fixed or random effects, and its description of time trends, do not match its own figures (reporting issues on the study card).

indirectness.note: The population, exposure and outcome are those of the claim: people who had just started cocaine, by form used, meeting dependence criteria.

imprecision.note: The powder-then-crack estimates rest on 9 to 96 people per year-pair, with intervals as wide as 9.2% to 64.5%.

publication_bias.note: Not applicable: one analysis of a national survey series.

large_effect.note: Descriptive claims are not upgraded for a large effect (METHODS §6.3).

grade.reasoning: A descriptive claim (relation 'describes') about how many people meet dependence criteria starts low (METHODS §6.3). Risk of bias −1, inconsistency −1 and imprecision −1 take it below the floor: very low. Status single study: one analysis of one survey series. The direction of the powder-crack difference agrees with an earlier analysis by the same research group of 1995–1998 survey data (Chen & Anthony, 2004, used in the answer on crack and powder), which is not independent, and a 2017 systematic review, which includes the 2004 analysis but predates this one, describes crack-versus-other-cocaine comparisons on dependence as mixed (Butler et al., 2017). statement: As described in two narrative reviews (Buchanan & Lavonas, 2012; Roberts & Chévez-Barrios, 2015; no systematic search or appraisal; all figures second-hand), levamisole, a veterinary medicine used mainly against worms in cattle, sheep and pigs and formerly used in people for autoimmune conditions and some cancers, was found in much of the cocaine sold in the United States around 2010: the US Drug Enforcement Administration first detected it in seized cocaine in 2003 and, by a figure the review does not source, in 73.2% of the cocaine it analysed in January 2010; in illicit cocaine samples analysed in Luxembourg it was the most abundant adulterant, though at low concentrations (1.5% to 4.1%); studies published in 2011 found it in 78% (Denver) and 88% (San Francisco) of urine samples that screened positive for cocaine metabolites; and the later review states that about 70% of US cocaine contains it. Case reports and small series from 2009 onward describe two conditions in people who had smoked, injected or snorted cocaine. One is agranulocytosis, a severe fall in the neutrophil white blood cells that fight infection, first reported in 2009 from Alberta, British Columbia, New Mexico, Washington, Arizona and Colorado; most cases followed smoking, although the earlier review says it is unclear whether smoking carries a greater risk than other routes. Neutrophil counts recovered within about 2 to 3 days of hospital treatment with GCSF in most case reports and within about 5 to 10 days after exposure ended without it, and about half of the patients in one series had more than one episode when they used cocaine again. The other is a skin vasculopathy, described in many anecdotal reports since 2009: painful purple patches in a net-like or star-shaped pattern, sometimes with blisters and dead skin, typically on the ears, cheeks, nose and limbs, with autoantibodies (such as ANCA), clotted small vessels and/or inflamed vessel walls on biopsy, and neutropenia in about half of cases; women made up most of the reported cases although more men use cocaine. The lesions usually resolved within a few weeks after cocaine use stopped, though some patients needed removal of dead tissue, skin grafts or amputation; no treatment has been tested in a controlled study. The reviews tie the cases to levamisole mainly by their pattern, by the person's cocaine use (by history or a urine test for a cocaine metabolite) and by the same effects seen when levamisole was used as a medicine. Laboratory confirmation of levamisole is mentioned for the first in-depth case report, in early 2010, and for one pictured patient, and neither review says how many of the reported cases had it measured. Serum testing is likely to be negative more than a day after the last exposure (plasma half-life about 5.6 hours, a figure the earlier review does not source), and preliminary evidence suggests that urine stays positive for about 2 to 3 days in most patients; the earlier review considers specific testing possibly unnecessary in many cases, and the later review states that it is not needed for diagnosis, because levamisole is so common in cocaine and the diagnosis can be made from the other findings, and that finding levamisole in patients' urine confirmed it as the cause. Because most people who use cocaine would test positive, a positive test shows exposure rather than cause (editors' note). A brain disorder (leukoencephalopathy) was linked to levamisole as a medicine, but the earlier review reports that no case acquired through cocaine had been reported, apart from one probable case at the authors' institution given without details, although its summary lists it among the consequences. Neither review gives how often these conditions occur among people exposed to levamisole through cocaine or weighs cocaine itself as a cause: the earlier review's statement that a significant minority of exposed people will be affected has no number behind it, its judgment that the skin condition is much more common with levamisole in cocaine than with the medicine rests on counts of anecdotal reports, and the later review's statement that the incidence is rising has no data behind it.
plain: Levamisole is a medicine used to treat worms in farm animals that was once also used in people. Around 2010 it was found in about 7 in 10 samples of cocaine tested by US drug police, and in about 8 or 9 in 10 urine samples that tested positive for cocaine in two US cities. Since 2009, case reports have described two kinds of harm in people who used cocaine. In some, the white blood cells that fight infection fell very low; the counts came back about 5 to 10 days after the exposure stopped, or within 2 to 3 days with a medicine given in hospital, and about half of the people in one series had it happen again when they used cocaine again. Others had painful purple patches on the skin, sometimes with dying skin, often on the ears, cheeks, nose, arms or legs; most healed within a few weeks after cocaine use stopped, but some people needed skin grafts or an amputation. These cases were linked to levamisole mainly because the person had used cocaine and because the same problems were seen when levamisole was a medicine. The reviews do not say how often levamisole itself was measured, and since most cocaine contained it, finding it shows that a person was exposed, not that it caused the harm. How often this harm happens to people exposed to levamisole is not known: the sources are case reports, described second-hand in two reviews.
population: People who had used cocaine and developed agranulocytosis or a skin vasculopathy, in case reports and small series from 2009 onward (Canada and US states), as described in two narrative reviews; seized cocaine (US Drug Enforcement Administration, Luxembourg) and urine samples screening positive for cocaine metabolites (Denver, San Francisco)
exposure: Levamisole, a veterinary deworming medicine, as an adulterant of cocaine (exposure inferred from cocaine use; levamisole measured in some reports, how many is not stated)
comparator: None (case reports and series; no group of exposed people without complications)
outcome: How often levamisole was found in cocaine and in urine; the clinical, laboratory and tissue picture of agranulocytosis and skin vasculopathy, and recovery after exposure ended
magnitude: Second-hand. Levamisole in 73.2% of cocaine analysed by the US DEA in January 2010 (unsourced); in about 70% of US cocaine (2015 review); the most abundant adulterant in cocaine samples analysed in Luxembourg, at low concentrations (1.5% to 4.1%); in 78% (Denver) and 88% (San Francisco) of urine samples screening positive for cocaine metabolites (studies published in 2011). How often harm occurs among exposed people: not given by either source. Recovery in case reports: neutrophils within 2 to 3 days with GCSF in most reports, 5 to 10 days after exposure ended without it; skin lesions usually within a few weeks of stopping cocaine. Neutropenia in about half of vasculopathy cases; repeat agranulocytosis in about half of one series with renewed cocaine use. Testing: serum likely negative more than 24 hours after the last exposure (plasma half-life about 5.6 hours); urine positive for about 2 to 3 days in most patients (preliminary evidence); how many reported cases had levamisole measured is not given.

risk_of_bias.note: Case reports and small series, summarized without appraisal by two narrative reviews (editors' narrative-review checklist high on cards sc_buchanan_2012 and sc_roberts_2015); attribution to levamisole rests mostly on cocaine use, the clinical pattern and the known effects of medical levamisole, and neither review says how many cases had levamisole measured.

inconsistency.note: The clinical picture is described consistently by both reviews; the figures for how much cocaine contained levamisole come from different places, years and measures and are reported as such.

indirectness.note: Second-hand through two narrative reviews (METHODS §6.3); the prevalence figures come from US seizures and two US hospital populations around 2008–2011 and may not describe cocaine elsewhere or today.

imprecision.note: No estimate is pooled or claimed; how often harm occurs is stated as unknown.

publication_bias.note: Case reports favour severe and well-documented cases; not rated separately, because the claim makes no statement about frequency.

grade.reasoning: Descriptive evidence from case reports, case series and drug and urine testing starts low; down one for risk of bias and one for indirectness: very low. The claim rests only on narrative reviews, so it stays at draft and its statement says that its figures are second-hand (METHODS §6.3). Status replicated for the clinical picture: case reports and series from several independent teams in Canada and at least four US states are described consistently by both reviews, which share that case literature and so count once; how often harm occurs among exposed people, and whether levamisole rather than cocaine causes it in a given person, are not established and are stated as unknown. The primary case series and urine studies (for example the 2011 Denver and San Francisco studies, and Buchanan et al.'s 2010 confirmed case) have not been read.
