statement: In people with lifetime cocaine use seen in treatment settings (17 studies, 5286 people, recruited, by the review's description, mostly through outpatient addiction treatment, with one inpatient service, although two studies' titles name therapeutic communities and one was a laboratory study; across all 20 included studies, 12 or 13 from the USA and 4 or 5 from Spain (the review counts 13 and 4, but its corrigendum moves one study to Europe) and one each from Canada, Brazil and the French Caribbean, mean age 37 and 68% men; people with primary psychotic disorders excluded), one meta-analysis of studies published to August 2020 found that how common cocaine-induced psychosis is depends on how it is defined (Sabe et al., 2021). In 13 studies that asked about psychotic symptoms with cocaine (questionnaires such as the Cocaine Experience Questionnaire, which mainly asks about paranoia and also about hallucinations, or study-specific questions, in two studies a single symptom), a pooled 68.4% (95% CI 62.8 to 73.5; I² 89%) reported having had them; in 4 studies that used diagnostic interviews (PRISM or MINI) for a DSM cocaine-induced psychotic disorder, 16% (10.6 to 23.2; I² 89%; 8.5 to 28.3 with a between-study variance estimated within that subgroup alone, editors' calculation) met the criteria; by instrument the figures ranged from 11.7% (PRISM, 3 studies) to 84.2% (SAPS-CIP, a single study that counted one psychotic symptom as a case), and by region from 30.7% in Europe to 67.9% in North America, as corrected by the authors (Sabe et al., 2022). The single pooled lifetime figure of 55.6% combines these definitions (I² 97%), and its printed interval (50.2 to 61.0) is narrower than a standard random-effects interval (46.0 to 64.8; editors' calculation). The figure for current use (50.2%, 32.0 to 68.4) rests on 102 people in three studies, two of them laboratory cocaine-challenge studies in which 12 of 28 and 29 of 44 participants had psychotic symptoms (paranoia, by the studies' titles) and one a psychiatric emergency series (12 of 30), so it is not a prevalence among people who currently use cocaine. Other drug use was common where reported (lifetime dependence on alcohol 56.5% in 3 studies, cannabis 32% and opioids 30% in 2) and could not be separated from cocaine, and neither could amount or route; the authors write that they cannot be certain cocaine is directly responsible, although they argue that alcohol and opioids are less likely to cause such symptoms and that cannabis is very unlikely to explain the findings (one included study found no significant effect of other substance use disorders after adjusting for age and sex); they add that treatment samples may inflate the figures (selection and Berkson bias) while people's limited insight into their symptoms may deflate them, and that cross-sectional studies with mostly retrospective assessment make conclusions about cause difficult. Two reports with identical counts may count the same 243 people twice (without one of them, 67.7% for symptoms, editors' calculation), and two studies, including the largest (2192 people), have no entry in the reference list. The review states, citing other work, that such symptoms are usually transient and pass with abstinence but can become more severe with continued use and last many weeks after the last use, and that a 2020 meta-analysis found no study of how often cocaine-induced psychotic disorder turns into schizophrenia; it did not measure either itself. The authors' corrigendum (Sabe et al., 2022) corrects only the regional figures (one study had been placed in the wrong region) and states that the conclusions are unchanged; it does not address the missing abstract, the two studies missing from the reference list, the possibly duplicated study or the shared between-study variance, so the other figures stand as printed.
plain: The answer depends on how psychosis is measured. In a review of 17 studies of 5,286 people, mostly in treatment for cocaine use in the USA and Spain, about 68 in 100 said that cocaine had at some time given them psychotic symptoms, such as paranoia, when asked with questionnaires; when strict diagnostic interviews were used, about 16 in 100 had a cocaine-induced psychotic disorder. Figures were lower in the European studies than in the North American ones. Many of these people were also dependent on alcohol or other drugs, which the review could not separate from cocaine, so it cannot show that cocaine alone caused the symptoms; and people in treatment may differ from others who use cocaine. The review says, citing other work, that such symptoms usually pass when cocaine use stops, although they can get worse with continued use and last for weeks, and that no study has measured how often a cocaine-induced psychotic disorder turns into schizophrenia; it did not study either itself. The authors later corrected their figures by region; the other figures stand.
population: People with lifetime cocaine use in treatment settings (17 studies, 5286 people, mostly drug treatment services in the USA and Spain, described by the review as outpatient), people with primary psychotic disorders excluded; and 102 people in three studies of current use (two laboratory cocaine-challenge studies and one psychiatric emergency series)
exposure: Cocaine use (cocaine dependence by DSM-III or DSM-IV in each study)
outcome: Cocaine-induced psychotic symptoms (questionnaires or study-specific questions, mostly about lifetime experience) or DSM cocaine-induced psychotic disorder (PRISM or MINI interviews)
magnitude: Lifetime, treatment samples: psychotic symptoms 68.4% (95% CI 62.8 to 73.5; 13 studies; I² 89%; prediction interval 47.8% to 83.6%, editors' calculation); DSM cocaine-induced psychotic disorder 16% (10.6 to 23.2; 4 studies; I² 89%; 8.5 to 28.3 with its own between-study variance, editors' calculation); both combined 55.6% (printed 50.2 to 61.0; standard random effects 46.0 to 64.8, prediction interval 18.7% to 87.2%, editors' calculation; the corrigendum's regional figure prints 46.6 to 64.2 for the same 17 studies); by instrument 11.7% (PRISM) to 84.2% (SAPS-CIP, one study); by region, as corrected (Sabe et al., 2022), North America 67.9% (57.0 to 77.2), South America and the Caribbean 56.1%, Europe 30.7% (18.7 to 46.1), I² 85%, 78% and 98% (the uncorrected article printed 66.5% and 25.1%). Current use (3 studies, 102 people, mostly laboratory): 50.2% (32.0 to 68.4), not a population prevalence. Without the possibly duplicated study: symptoms 67.7% (62.1 to 72.9).

risk_of_bias.note: Cross-sectional studies in treatment samples, mostly with retrospective self-report of symptoms (selection and Berkson bias named by the authors); two reports may count the same 243 people twice; the review is of critically low confidence on AMSTAR 2 (card sc_sabe_2021), and its corrigendum corrects only the regional figures.

inconsistency.note: I² 89% within each definition and 97% overall; figures differ by instrument (11.7% to 84.2%) and by region (Europe 30.7%, North America 67.9%, as corrected), largely unexplained.

indirectness.note: Treatment samples, mostly in the USA and Spain, not people who use cocaine in general; other drug use was common and could not be separated, so the symptoms are attributed to cocaine by the people asked or by the interviewer.

imprecision.note: The definition-specific intervals are moderately narrow; the overall printed interval understates the spread (editors' calculation) and is not used as the headline figure.

publication_bias.note: Not investigated by the review; not rated down, because prevalence studies are unlikely to be published according to the prevalence they find.

grade.reasoning: Prevalence figures are descriptive (relation 'describes') and start low; down one each for risk of bias, inconsistency and indirectness, which is below the floor: very low. Status replicated: within each definition, independent studies agree in order of magnitude (13 symptom studies, prediction interval about 48% to 84%, editors' calculation; 4 diagnostic studies, 10% to 36%), the spread being rated under inconsistency; Cubells 2005 and Tang 2007 may be one sample and are counted once. The current-use figure is not used as a prevalence. The authors' corrigendum (Sabe et al., 2022), now read, corrects only the regional figures and changes no rating; the primary studies, the review's supplementary tables and the 2020 meta-analysis on transition (card sc_murrie_2020, on the methamphetamine page) were not used here.

statement: In the nine placebo-controlled randomized trials published up to 2006 and pooled in one review (640 patients with cocaine dependence, 344 given a stimulant medicine and 296 placebo, all with psychological treatment as well), stimulant medicines did not detectably reduce how many people dropped out (relative risk 0.97, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.10, with no difference for any single medicine) or the proportion of urine samples positive for a cocaine breakdown product in the trials that reported it (0.94, 0.84 to 1.05 across six trials; 0.84, 0.67 to 1.04 leaving out bupropion; one dexamphetamine trial entered this main analysis with its per-protocol sample of 62 of 94 randomized). Only an exploratory analysis, which filled in cocaine use for three further trials as the average of their starting and final values and used per-protocol rather than all-randomized data for two dexamphetamine trials, found fewer positive samples with dexamphetamine (0.73, 0.60 to 0.90) and with the medicines pooled (0.87, 0.77 to 0.99); that signal rests on filled-in outcomes, on two trials by one research group, and in part on one treatment arm in which 42 of 46 people dropped out (without that arm, 0.79, 0.62 to 1.00, for dexamphetamine and 0.93, 0.84 to 1.03, for the medicines pooled; editors' calculation), and the review's own authors call per-protocol bias unlikely without testing it. Modafinil's estimate in the main analysis was not significant (0.73, 0.50 to 1.04). More people stopped taking a stimulant than placebo because of unwanted effects (15 of 344, 4.4%, against 4 of 296, 1.4%, printed as 1.3%; p = 0.03), though which effects led people to stop was generally not described; the unwanted effects most commonly reported were sleeping problems, anxiety and jitteriness. The review's statement that no serious unwanted effect was reported has no counterpart in its results, its Discussion describes the information on unwanted effects as too limited for conclusions, and several trials did not say how they were assessed. The trials were small (30 to 149 patients, 42 to 182 days), nearly 9 in 10 participants were men, about half were also dependent on opioids and, in the four trials that reported route, most smoked or injected cocaine, and the review calculates that 144 to 584 patients per arm would have been needed to detect a difference, more than any trial had; its own confidence was rated critically low, and the two headline figures printed in its abstract appear nowhere in its results. Craving could not be pooled. This is the evidence up to 2006 only: later reviews of these medicines, including modafinil and methylphenidate, have not been read. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: Do stimulant medicines help people stop using cocaine? In nine trials up to 2006, with 640 people who all also had talking therapy, people given a stimulant medicine did no better than people given a dummy pill: there was no clear difference in staying in treatment or in urine tests positive for cocaine, though the trials were too small to rule out a modest benefit. One extra analysis, which filled in missing results and, for two trials, left out some of the people who had been randomized, did find fewer positive tests with dexamphetamine, but that result is not reliable. More people stopped the medicine because of unwanted effects: about 4 in 100, against about 1 in 100 on the dummy pill; the most common unwanted effects were trouble sleeping, anxiety and feeling jittery. The trials were small, most of the people were men, and about half also had problems with opioids. Newer reviews of these medicines have not been read yet.
population: 640 patients with cocaine dependence in nine double-blind placebo-controlled randomized trials published up to 2006 (30 to 149 patients each, 42 to 182 days): 11.9% women, mean age 34.9, 65.3% using crack (five trials reporting), 51.4% smoking and 35.8% injecting (four trials reporting), 46.9% also opioid-dependent (mostly in three trials requiring both), every trial adding psychological treatment
exposure: A central nervous system stimulant medicine taken daily by mouth: mazindol (2 trials), dexamphetamine (3), methylphenidate (2), modafinil (1) or bupropion (1), at each trial's doses
comparator: Placebo with the same psychological treatment in the same trial
outcome: Dropping out of the trial; the proportion of urine samples positive for benzoylecgonine; craving; dropping out because of unwanted effects
magnitude: Castells et al. (2007), random-effects relative risks, medicine against placebo. Dropout: all stimulants 0.97 (95% CI 0.85 to 1.10), I² 0%; without bupropion 0.97 (0.85 to 1.11); dexamphetamine 0.90 (0.71 to 1.12); methylphenidate 1.15 (0.77 to 1.73); modafinil 1.07 (0.55 to 2.09); mazindol 0.93 (0.59 to 1.47); bupropion 0.86 (0.41 to 1.79); 167 of 344 against 138 of 296 dropped out. Cocaine-positive urine, main analysis of six trials: all stimulants 0.94 (0.84 to 1.05); without bupropion 0.84 (0.67 to 1.04); modafinil 0.73 (0.50 to 1.04), p = 0.08; dexamphetamine 0.81 (0.56 to 1.16); methylphenidate 1.09 (0.72 to 1.64); mazindol 0.53 (0.11 to 2.54); bupropion 0.98 (0.86 to 1.12). Exploratory analysis of nine trials with filled-in values: dexamphetamine 0.73 (0.60 to 0.90), p = 0.003; all stimulants 0.87 (0.77 to 0.99); without bupropion 0.82 (0.71 to 0.94); leaving out the one arm in which 42 of 46 people dropped out, the dexamphetamine estimate becomes 0.79 (0.62 to 1.00) (study card's calculation) and the pooled estimate for all stimulants 0.93 (0.84 to 1.03) (editors' calculation). Grabowski 2004 entered the main urine analysis with its per-protocol sample (62 of 94 randomized). Post hoc, the three trials requiring both cocaine and opioid dependence: dropout 0.85 (0.56 to 1.30), cocaine use 0.86 (0.68 to 1.09). Dropout for unwanted effects 15 of 344 (4.4%) against 4 of 296 (1.4%, editors' arithmetic; printed as 1.3%), p = 0.03. Absolute risks for the efficacy outcomes are not reported.

evidence.extracted: Systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of double-blind, placebo-controlled, parallel-group randomized trials of a central nervous system stimulant in patients with cocaine dependence: three databases searched from 1966 to November 2006, reference lists hand-searched and first authors contacted; 584 citations screened, 33 potentially eligible, 9 included (11 medicine-placebo comparisons), with unpublished data obtained for four trials. Trials of people with cocaine abuse rather than dependence were excluded. Outcomes: dropout, cocaine use as the proportion of urine samples positive for benzoylecgonine, craving and dropout for unwanted effects.

risk_of_bias.note: Randomized and double-blind, but the review's confidence is AMSTAR 2 critically low on its study card: no protocol, no list of excluded trials, a reporting-quality scale instead of a risk-of-bias assessment, an outcome that treats each group's proportion of positive urine samples as if it were a proportion of patients, per-protocol data pooled with all-randomized data, about 48% dropout in both arms and no examination of unblinding by the medicines' own effects.

inconsistency.note: I² 0% for dropout and consistent null estimates across five medicines in the main analysis; the only estimate pointing to benefit comes from the exploratory analysis with imputed outcomes, which the claim reports as such.

indirectness.note: Not downgraded: the claim is worded for the people, medicines, comparison and outcomes of these trials, and says in its population that 11.9% were women, about half were also opioid-dependent and most smoked or injected cocaine, that every trial added psychological treatment and that follow-up ran to at most 182 days. The handling of the cocaine-use outcome (each group's proportion of positive urine samples entered as if it were a proportion of patients, and per-protocol data pooled with all-randomized data) is rated once, under risk of bias, not twice (METHODS §6.3). That the evidence stops in 2006 is a matter of currency, flagged in the claim and in its verification note rather than rated here.

imprecision.note: 640 patients in all against the review's own estimate of 144 to 584 per arm; the intervals around the null estimates (0.85 to 1.10 for dropout, 0.84 to 1.05 for cocaine use, 0.67 to 1.04 without bupropion) still allow reductions of up to about a third in cocaine-positive samples, so this is a failure to detect a difference, not a demonstration that none exists.

publication_bias.note: Not investigated by the review; its searches covered three databases with contact with first authors, and eight of nine trials were publicly funded.

grade.reasoning: Randomized evidence starts high. Risk of bias −1 (the review's handling of the cocaine-use outcome and of per-protocol data, about 48% dropout in both arms, and its critically low AMSTAR 2 confidence) and imprecision −1 (intervals that still allow a clinically meaningful reduction, against the review's own estimate that 144 to 584 patients per arm would be needed) give low certainty; indirectness is not downgraded, because the claim is worded for the people and outcomes of these trials and the outcome's handling is already counted under risk of bias. Worded as no detectable difference, not as equivalence, as METHODS §6.3 requires: the interval does not exclude a worthwhile benefit. Status replicated: nine independent trials of five medicines point the same way on dropout and on the main cocaine-use outcome. Not used, following the study card: the exploratory dexamphetamine and pooled estimates as evidence of efficacy, the abstract's headline figures, and its statement that no serious unwanted effect occurred.

verification.flag_note: The evidence ends in 2006. Four later reviews on the project's cocaine list have not been read and could change this answer: Pérez-Mañá et al. (2011, indirect dopamine agonists), Sangroula et al. (2017, modafinil), Biso et al. (2025, methylphenidate) and Paterson et al. (2026, pharmacological interventions for cocaine use disorder). This claim is about medicines tried for cocaine dependence as studied in trials; it reports what was given to patients and what was measured.

statement: In seven cohorts of people with problematic or dependent cocaine use, studied between 1985 and 2005 in the USA (two cohorts), Canada, France, the Netherlands, Brazil and Italy and summarized without pooling in one systematic review (Degenhardt et al., 2011; figures second-hand, several of them supplied by the cohorts' investigators as personal communications), deaths were 4.4 to 7.7 times as frequent as in the general population of the same age and sex in the four cohorts that reported standardized mortality ratios (SMR): 4.74 (95% CI 4.19 to 5.29) among 717 people injecting cocaine in Vancouver; 4.36 among men and 7.70 among women in a French national cohort of 2212 people arrested for using or dealing cocaine or crack; 4.75 (2.26 to 9.96) among men in treatment for cocaine dependence in Italy (mostly intranasal use by one of the review's two descriptions, crack dependence by the other); and 7.60 at five years among 131 people treated for crack dependence in São Paulo. Crude death rates ranged from about 0.5 to 6.2 per 100 person-years, that is about 5 to 62 deaths per 1,000 people per year: 6.16 in the Vancouver cohort; 4.69 among people injecting cocaine only and 4.37 among people injecting cocaine and heroin in Baltimore; 4.6 among HIV-negative people mainly injecting cocaine in the Netherlands (9 deaths); 3.51 in the São Paulo crack cohort and 3.53 among people using cocaine daily without injecting, presumed to smoke crack, in Seattle (3 deaths; the review notes that this group is not independent of the cohort's injecting group); and 0.69 in the French arrest cohort and 0.50 in the Italian treatment cohort. Where it was examined, death rates were 2.0 to 2.4 times as high in people with HIV (Vancouver 9.83 against 4.91 per 100 person-years; Baltimore 7.74 and 7.98 against 3.25 and 3.45; ratios by editors' calculation). Among people who injected, AIDS and overdose were the commonest causes of death in both cohorts that reported causes, followed by infections linked to injecting (sepsis or endocarditis) in Baltimore and by injuries in Vancouver (Baltimore, people injecting cocaine only: AIDS 62 of 175 deaths, overdose 20, sepsis or endocarditis 15, cancer 13, injuries 12, liver or gastrointestinal disease 10, heart disease 7, suicide 2; Vancouver: overdose 53, AIDS 30 and injuries 23 of 158 deaths); among people treated for crack dependence in Brazil the commonest were gunshot wounds (10 of 23 deaths) and AIDS (6); and in the Italian cohort of 309 men with 7 deaths, cause-specific SMRs were 14.85 (4.79 to 46.04) for vascular disease, 9.95 (1.40 to 70.61) for overdose and 7.07 (1 to 50.16) for suicide. The SMRs take only age and sex into account, so they describe the excess deaths in these groups, not an effect of cocaine itself apart from injecting, HIV, heroin and alcohol use and social disadvantage; the authors suggest the differences in crude death rates between cohorts may reflect general health, route of use, HIV, access to care and possibly social disadvantage, and say they cannot tell which. All the cohorts came from injecting, treatment or arrest settings, mostly socially disadvantaged and several with high HIV prevalence, the effect of HIV treatment could not be examined, and no cohort followed people who only snort cocaine (the authors think it likely, citing another study, that their mortality is much lower, but there are no data). How deaths were identified and causes assigned is not reported for the cohorts, and the review's figures have inconsistencies: the crude rate printed for people injecting cocaine daily in Seattle (0.53 per 100 person-years) does not match its own 3 deaths in 319 person-years, which give 0.94 (editors' calculation), and the Italian men's SMR is 4.75 in the table but 4.6 in the Discussion.
plain: In seven groups of people studied in six countries between 1985 and 2005 (people who injected cocaine, smoked crack every day, were treated for cocaine or crack dependence, or were arrested for cocaine offences), between about 5 and 62 in every 1,000 died each year, depending on the group. In the four groups compared with the general population of the same age and sex, 4 to 8 times as many died as expected. Among people who injected, AIDS and overdose were the main causes, then infections linked to injecting or injuries; among people treated for crack dependence in Brazil, gunshot wounds and AIDS. Where it was looked at, death rates were 2 to 2.4 times as high in people with HIV. Many people in these groups also injected heroin or had HIV, and the comparison took only age and sex into account, so these figures do not show what cocaine itself does. No group of people who only snort cocaine has been followed. The figures come from one review that did not combine them, and some were sent by the researchers rather than published.
population: People with problematic or dependent cocaine use in seven cohorts (injecting cocaine, smoking crack daily, in treatment for cocaine or crack dependence, or arrested for cocaine offences) in the USA, Canada, France, the Netherlands, Brazil and Italy, studied between 1985 and 2005
exposure: Problematic or dependent cocaine use as each cohort defined it at baseline (route: injecting or smoking crack in most cohorts; mostly intranasal in one treatment cohort by one of the review's descriptions; not stated for the arrest cohort)
comparator: The general population of the same age and sex (standardized mortality ratios, four cohorts); none for crude rates; within cohorts, people with and without HIV
outcome: All-cause mortality (crude rate per 100 person-years; standardized mortality ratio) and causes of death
magnitude: Second-hand, not pooled. SMR against the general population of the same age and sex (4 cohorts): 4.74 (4.19 to 5.29), people injecting cocaine, Vancouver; 4.36 (men) and 7.70 (women), people arrested for cocaine offences, France; 4.75 (2.26 to 9.96), men in treatment, Italy; 7.60 at 5 years, people treated for crack dependence, São Paulo. Crude mortality about 0.5 to 6.2 per 100 person-years (about 5 to 62 per 1,000 per year), by cohort as in the statement; with HIV 9.83 against 4.91 (Vancouver) and 7.7 to 8.0 against 3.3 to 3.5 (Baltimore) per 100 person-years (2.0 to 2.4 times as high, editors' calculation). Causes as in the statement.

evidence.locator: 2.5 Reporting of mortality estimates, 1st to 3rd paragraphs
evidence.extracted: Crude mortality rates (deaths per 100 person-years) were taken as reported or calculated from deaths and person-years, assuming deaths at mid-follow-up where only total years were reported; SMRs (deaths relative to those expected among people of the same age and sex in the country's general population) were taken as reported by four cohorts. No pooled estimates were made because the studies were few, their populations varied and their statistics were limited.

grade.reasoning: Standardized mortality ratios and crude death rates are descriptive (relation 'describes', METHODS §6.3): they start low and are not upgraded. statement: In cross-sectional studies, people with a diagnosis of cocaine abuse, dependence or use disorder (and, in some pooled studies, people who used cocaine recreationally) score lower on average than comparison groups who do not use cocaine on tests of memory, attention, holding back a response and decision making. Most pooled differences are small to moderate, about 0.2 to 0.6 standard deviations, but the studies disagree, and none of the designs can show that cocaine caused the differences or that scores recover with time off cocaine. Five reviews, all rated critically low confidence on AMSTAR 2, cover overlapping literatures. The largest pooled analysis, a 2014 meta-analysis of 46 studies (1452 people with a diagnosed cocaine use disorder, 1411 healthy controls), gives differences of 0.22 to 0.59 across 11 domains for studies with abstinence under 12 weeks (heterogeneity significant in 5) and 0.04 to 0.53 for studies of people with positive urine tests. A 2026 meta-analysis of 20 studies of laboratory inhibition tasks gives g = 0.65 (95% CI 0.28 to 1.03; I² 83.6%; 95% prediction interval −0.95 to 2.26) with significant funnel asymmetry (Egger p = .008), but two small studies entered there with effects of 3.1 to 4.9 report about 0.74 and 1.4 themselves (Lane et al., 2007; Hester & Garavan, 2004; editors' calculations from their printed test statistics), and the review's value for Lane et al. is reproduced exactly when that study's standard errors are read as standard deviations; with the two corrected, the editors' recalculation of the review's aggregated model gives 0.46 (0.25 to 0.67), I² about 66%, prediction interval about −0.31 to 1.23 by the review's own method (−0.37 to 1.28 with a t quantile), and Egger's test is no longer significant (p = 0.12). Two earlier reviews give a median difference of 0.35 across 140 test measures, 93 of them each resting on a single small study (2005), and pooled differences of 0.24 to 1.22 in absolute size from three to nine studies per outcome, after studies that raised heterogeneity were dropped from four of eight pools and with no heterogeneity statistics printed (2013). A 2018 critical review of 47 studies argues that the evidence does not support broad deficits, mainly because 13 of its 22 neuropsychological studies did not compare scores with test norms and some did not match groups on age (5) or education (6) or control for other drug use (8); its own table nonetheless lists poorer performance of a cocaine group in at least one area in 19 of the 21 studies with a comparison group (the first reader's count). Where that review reports a comparison with norms, the differences were small: mild impairment, less than 1 standard deviation below the comparison mean, in a PET study using age-adjusted scores, and scores not outside the normative range in two studies (one of people who used cocaine recreationally), although in both the cocaine group also did worse than its comparison group on some measures. Most pooled differences are smaller than 1 standard deviation, the distance below test norms (a T score below 40) that the 2018 review proposes for calling a score impaired; how many individuals fell below such a cut-off is not reported. Abstinence at testing varies from current use to several years, and in the 2013 and 2018 reviews a substantial minority of studies tested people within 72 hours of last use or with positive urine tests. In the 5 studies with abstinence over 20 weeks the 2014 meta-analysis found a composite difference of 0.19 (95% CI −0.006 to 0.391; P = 0.057), which its authors read as recovery after about 5 months; but these are different studies rather than the same people retested, the difference between the abstinence groups was not tested, people who relapse early are missing from long-term samples, and the 2026 meta-analysis found no moderation by days of abstinence. The cocaine groups often also used alcohol, cannabis or other drugs; in several studies the comparison groups were younger or had more education (in 11 of the 2026 review's 24 studies the groups differed in education, age, sex or ethnicity, or were poorly matched), and the pooled estimates are unadjusted group differences. The one study read in full that retested people, after four weeks of enforced abstinence, had no group of people who do not use cocaine, and within it heavier reported drinking and heavier reported cocaine use predicted different tests (Bolla et al., 2000). Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
plain: Does cocaine affect memory and thinking? On average, people with cocaine problems score somewhat lower than people who do not use cocaine on tests of memory, attention, holding back a response and decision making. Most gaps are small to medium, and studies disagree about their size. The newest review got the numbers of two small studies wrong, which made its average gap look bigger; with them corrected, the gap is smaller. People were tested after they had been using, so the tests cannot show that cocaine caused the gap: it may have been there before. Many people who used cocaine also drank or used other drugs, some were tested within three days of last use, and in several studies the comparison groups were younger or had more schooling. Most studies did not compare scores with the usual range for people of the same age and schooling. In studies of people who had stopped for more than about 5 months the gap was small, but these were different people, not the same people tested again, so they do not show that scores get better after stopping.
population: Adults with a DSM diagnosis of cocaine abuse, dependence or cocaine use disorder, mostly in treatment or research samples (some pooled studies also include people who used cocaine recreationally), in most studies tested once, from current use to several years of abstinence; three primary studies read in full: 15 people tested 12 to 72 hours after use (Hester & Garavan, 2004), 18 people with current dependence, 15 of them urine-positive (Lane et al., 2007), and 56 people who all used cocaine, tested 1 to 3 days and 4 weeks into an inpatient stay (Bolla et al., 2000)
exposure: Regular cocaine use (most samples meeting DSM criteria for abuse, dependence or use disorder; some recreational samples); in one study, grams per week derived from reported weekly spending
comparator: People without cocaine use (healthy or drug-free control groups), recruited separately, in several studies younger or with more education; in Bolla et al. (2000), no group of people who do not use cocaine (people with more and less reported use within the same sample)
outcome: Neuropsychological and laboratory task scores (memory, attention, inhibition, decision making, psychomotor speed)
magnitude: Each review's signs are given as printed, with their direction. Jovanovski et al. (2005; 15 studies published 1992–2002, 481 against 586; signs follow each test's scoring): median absolute difference 0.35 across 140 measures, 93 of them each resting on a single study; multi-study measures Trail Making B 0.49 (9 estimates) and Trail Making A 0.19 (10); WAIS-R Digit Symbol −0.49 (6), Rey-Osterrieth delayed recall −0.45 (6) and WAIS-R Arithmetic −0.66 (5), lower scores in the cocaine groups, which the review reads as deficits; Stroop colour-word interference −0.11 (7), direction not stated; the largest values, about 1.0 to 1.1, from single small studies, the largest of them on a test the cocaine group did better on. Spronk et al. (2013), pooled standardized differences, all described by the authors as poorer performance in the cocaine groups (printed signs differ between outcomes): sustained attention −1.22 (−1.58 to −0.85), failed inhibitions 0.64 (0.44 to 0.84, 8 to 9 studies), stop-signal reaction time 0.50 (0.11 to 0.90, 3), immediate recall −0.46 (−0.70 to −0.23, 8), perseverative errors 0.37 (0.17 to 0.57, 5), reward-based decision making 0.53 (0.32 to 0.75, 7), psychomotor motor responses 0.75 (0.46 to 1.04, 3), psychomotor response time −0.24 (−0.47 to −0.02, 6); studies were dropped for heterogeneity in four of these pools and no I² is printed. Potvin et al. (2014; 46 studies, 1452 against 1411; positive = worse in the cocaine group): abstinence under 12 weeks, d from 0.219 (language/verbal) to 0.592 (attention) across 11 domains, every interval above zero, Q significant (P < 0.1) in 5; urine-positive studies, 0.042 to 0.534, intervals including zero in 5 of 11; abstinence over 20 weeks, one composite 0.193 (−0.006 to 0.391), P = 0.057, 5 studies, fixed effect. López-Martín et al. (2026; 20 studies, 23 effects; positive = worse in the cocaine group): g = 0.65 (0.28 to 1.03), I² 83.6%, prediction interval −0.95 to 2.26, leave-one-out 0.51 to 0.72, Egger p = .008; no moderator (sex, age, years of use, days of abstinence, clinical against community sample) was significant; 16 of 27 individual comparisons were significant, including 4 of 10 stop-signal studies; its criterion was at most two months of abstinence, but five included studies report average abstinence of 152 to 335 days; in the cocaine groups alcohol use was 6.7% to 100% and cannabis use 12.5% to 80%, with only cocaine listed for 7 of 24 studies. Two of its study values are not what the studies report: Lane et al. (2007), entered as 3.13, gives about 0.74 (hard No-Go trials, t(31) = −2.16), and Hester & Garavan (2004), entered as 3.39 to 4.90, about 1.4 (group F(1,28) = 15.03) (editors' calculations); with these corrected, the editors' recalculation gives 0.46 (0.25 to 0.67), I² about 66%, prediction interval about −0.31 to 1.23 by the review's own method (−0.37 to 1.28 with a t quantile), Egger p = 0.12 (without the two studies, 0.41, 0.20 to 0.62, Egger p = 0.31). Frazer et al. (2018): no pooling; 19 of 21 studies with a comparison group list poorer performance in at least one area (first reader's count); 13 of 22 did not interpret results against norms, 5 of 22 did not match on age, 6 of 22 on education and 8 of 22 did not control for other drug use; by the review's count 11 of 14 functional-imaging studies found no group difference on their cognitive task. Primary studies read in full: Hester & Garavan (2004; 15 against 15, tested 12 to 72 hours after use; education 11.5 against 13.9 years), group difference about 1.4; Lane et al. (2007; 18 against 15, 15 of them urine-positive; education 12.6 against 16.0 years), about 0.74 (editors' calculations). Bolla et al. (2000; 56 people, no group of people who do not use cocaine): at 1 to 3 days, drug-dose terms account for about 8% to 24% of the residual variance in the tests they predict (editors' calculation from the printed F statistics, by the study card, recomputed by the second reader and the adjudicator).

evidence.extracted: The paper concludes that using cocaine and alcohol together may have additive negative effects compared with using one of them, but every participant used cocaine, there is no group that used alcohol alone and no cocaine-by-alcohol interaction term is reported for the first session, so additivity is not tested in these data (study card). evidence.locator: Methods › Literature Search and Study Selection, 1st paragraph (p. 369); Methods › Quantitative Data Synthesis, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (pp. 369–370); Methods › Homogeneity of Effect-Size Estimates, 1st paragraph, and Results › Study Characteristics, 1st paragraph (p. 370)
evidence.extracted: Meta-analysis (Cohen's d, positive = worse performance in the group with cocaine use disorder) of 46 case–control studies published before 1 January 2013 (PubMed, Embase and Ovid, plus reference lists): 1452 people with a DSM-III or DSM-IV diagnosis of cocaine abuse or dependence and 1411 healthy controls. Excluded were samples with comorbid Axis I disorders, studies in which all participants used several substances, and testing during scanning. Tests were averaged within each study into domains and pooled with random effects; studies (or single tests) more than 2 SD from the overall composite were excluded as outliers. Studies were grouped by the abstinence each reported: short-term (urine positive for cocaine, under 72 hours), intermediate (under 12 weeks) and long-term (over 20 weeks); no study fell between 13 and 19 weeks, and meta-regression on abstinence was not used because its distribution across studies was skewed (Kolmogorov–Smirnov P = 0.0001). The review gives no table of its included studies, no appraisal of their quality and no assessment of publication bias.

risk_of_bias.note: Every comparison is cross-sectional with no measurement before use, and the pooled estimates are unadjusted group differences; groups differed in education or age in several studies (11 of 24 studies in the 2026 review; 5 and 6 of 22 in the 2018 review; 13.9 against 11.5 and 16.0 against 12.6 years of education in the two small studies read in full). Exposure is self-reported and, in one study read in full, derived from recalled spending. All five reviews are AMSTAR 2 critically low: only the 2026 review appraised its primary studies with a checklist (on which its two raters agreed poorly) and the 2018 review did so informally, two reviews dropped or omitted studies without a documented rule, and the 2026 review misentered the values of two studies.

inconsistency.note: I² 83.6% with a prediction interval from −0.95 to 2.26 in the newest meta-analysis, and still about 66% with a prediction interval of about −0.31 to 1.23 after its two misentered studies are corrected (editors' recalculation); in the 2014 meta-analysis heterogeneity was significant in 5 of 11 domains at abstinence under 12 weeks; the most-used tests in the 2005 review range from about 0.1 to 0.49 with wide spreads between studies; the 2013 and 2018 reviews read largely overlapping evidence in opposite directions.

indirectness.note: Mostly second-hand: most anchors are reviews' accounts of primary studies not read here (METHODS §6.3); the three primary studies read in full are two small comparisons of people tested within days of use (both misentered by the 2026 review) and one study without a group of people who do not use cocaine. Laboratory tasks, mostly without norms, so what the differences mean in daily life is not measured; a substantial minority of participants were tested within 72 hours of use or with positive urine, which mixes recent use and early withdrawal with any lasting difference.

imprecision.note: The pooled estimates rest on hundreds of people and most have intervals that exclude zero; imprecision is not rated down again, since the wide prediction intervals are rated under inconsistency.

publication_bias.note: Suspected: the literature consists of small case–control studies, and four of the five reviews did not assess publication bias. In the 2026 meta-analysis the significant funnel asymmetry (Egger p = .008) depended on two misentered studies; with them corrected the test is no longer significant (p = 0.12), but with 20 studies it has little power.

grade.reasoning: Cross-sectional evidence starts low. Risk of bias −1, inconsistency −1, indirectness −1 and publication bias −1 take it well below the floor: very low. The claim is worded as an association and is rated as one. Status mixed: the direction is reported consistently (lower scores in the cocaine groups in most pooled estimates, and in 19 of 21 studies in the 2018 review's table), but the size is not: study-level effects in the newest meta-analysis run from a significant difference favouring the cocaine group to large differences, heterogeneity remains after correction, the reviews of the same literature reach opposite conclusions about whether the differences amount to impairment, and the newest pooled estimate falls from 0.65 to about 0.46 when its two misentered studies are corrected. The five reviews are not independent: the 2013 review was written to follow on from the 2005 one, the 2014 meta-analysis pools studies to 2012 that include some of the 2005 review's, the 2018 review tabulates studies also covered by the 2013 one, and the 2026 meta-analysis covers the same literature without citing any of them (Lane et al., 2007, is inside both the 2014 and the 2026 pooled estimates); they are counted once. Not used, following the study cards: any statement that cocaine caused the differences; the 2005 review's abstract range for attention; the 2013 review's phrase about general impairment; the 2014 review's conclusion that cognition nearly returns to normal after about 5 months, which rests on one non-significant composite from 5 studies compared with other studies; the 2018 review's conclusion that there are no broad deficits, which its own tables do not support; the 2026 review's printed values for two studies, which their own reports contradict; and any claim about recovery with abstinence, which no design read can address.

verification.flag_note: Whether scores recover after stopping is not answered by any source read: the 2014 meta-analysis compares different studies grouped by abstinence (its long-term composite rests on 5 studies, P = 0.057), the 2026 meta-analysis's study-level moderator test is null on sparse data, and the one study with a retest (Bolla et al., 2000) had no group of people who do not use cocaine and could not separate practice effects from recovery. The primary studies behind the 2026 meta-analysis's two outlying values (Hester & Garavan, 2004; Lane et al., 2007) and the 2014 meta-analysis (Potvin et al., 2014) were read on 12 November 2026 by AI reader 392 (adjudicator); the new anchors and the editors' recalculation await a fresh reader's check.

statement: In adults who came to US hospital emergency departments with chest pain, or with other symptoms that can signal a heart problem, after recent cocaine use, a heart attack (acute myocardial infarction) was diagnosed in a small minority: from under 1 to about 6 in 100 of all the patients enrolled in four studies, and up to about 9 in 100 when only the patients kept in hospital, or those tested most fully, were counted. The share varied with whom each study included and with how heart attacks were looked for and defined. In a prospective study at six inner-city teaching hospitals in four US cities (COCHPA, April 1991 to May 1992), 14 of 246 enrolments of patients with chest pain who said they had used cocaine in the past week had an infarction (5.7%; 95% CI printed as 2.7% to 8.7%; exact 3.1% to 9.4%, editors' calculation; the paper calls the 246 patients, but at the four centres that continued into a one-year follow-up its 214 enrolments were 214 visits by 205 people, so some people were counted more than once; editors' comparison with Hollander et al., 1995c), defined as prolonged chest pain with CK-MB above the hospital's upper limit of normal (or ECG evolution) within 24 hours; CK-MB was measured when total CK was raised, and cardiac enzymes were measured at all in 215 patients and more than once in 151. The authors calculate 7.3% among patients with two or more measurements and 8.6% among admitted patients, and note that clinicians may not have told investigators about patients they judged at very low risk (Hollander et al., 1994). At one urban hospital in Flint, Michigan (July 1996 to February 1998) whose policy was to admit every such patient for at least 23 hours, with cardiac enzymes on arrival and every 8 hours for 24 hours, 15 of 250 admitted adults (6%) met World Health Organization criteria for infarction on serial CK-MB testing; the 95% confidence interval is printed as 3.1% to 8.9% in the Results and as 4.1% to 8.9% in the abstract, and the exact interval is 3.4% to 9.7% (editors' calculation) (Weber et al., 2000). Patients entered if they reported cocaine use in the previous week or had a positive urine screen (185 of the 196 tested were positive); they were young (mean age 33.5 years), mostly men (77%), African American (84%) and smoked tobacco (77%), and most had used cocaine within the previous 24 hours, mostly by smoking crack. They were found through hospital records coded for cocaine or other drug use: records coded for infarction were searched more thoroughly than others and 9 patients sent home from the emergency department were left out, both of which would tend to raise the share, whereas urine testing was routine only for patients aged 50 or under without cardiac risk factors, so older patients who had used cocaine may have been missed; the authors also cannot exclude that a few small infarctions were missed. At one hospital in Richmond, Virginia (January 1994 to June 1996), an infarction (CK-MB mass with a relative index, and a rise and fall) was diagnosed at 6 of 241 emergency visits by 218 patients with symptoms suggesting heart ischaemia after cocaine use, acknowledged by the patient or shown by a urine screen (2.5% of visits; 6 of 218 patients is 2.8%, editors' calculation, the figure the 2008 American Heart Association statement gives) and at 6 of the 69 visits admitted to the coronary care unit (8.7%); most lower-risk patients had a heart scan in the emergency department and went home without serial enzyme tests (Kontos et al., 1999). In a 1993 trial at 10 US hospitals with urban, suburban and semirural catchment areas, which enrolled emergency patients whose main complaint was chest pain, shortness of breath, dizziness, palpitations or other symptoms suggesting heart ischaemia, 293 of 10,689 (2.7%) reported recent cocaine use or tested positive; 2 of them (0.7%; exact 95% CI 0.08% to 2.4%) had an infarction by World Health Organization criteria (at least two of typical chest discomfort, changing ECGs and a rise and fall of cardiac markers), and 4 more had unstable angina. Serial enzyme results were available for 109 of the 127 admitted but more than one CK result for only 37 of the 166 sent home, and the authors suggest that their broader inclusion and different criteria for infarction may explain the sevenfold difference from two earlier prospective series (Feldman et al., 2000). At the Flint hospital in 1998–1999, 42 of 344 patients with chest pain who reported cocaine use in the previous week or had cocaine metabolites in urine were judged at high risk and admitted directly, and 10 of them had an infarction (Weber et al., 2003). Earlier retrospective series, as summarized by Weber et al. (2000), ranged from 0% to 31% depending on whom they enrolled; the 2008 scientific statement of the American Heart Association, a consensus document without a reported systematic search method, gives 0.7% to 6% (McCord et al., 2008). Few patients died in hospital. At the Flint hospital in 1996–1998 there were 7 complications (sustained ventricular tachycardia in 2 patients, supraventricular tachycardia in 3, heart failure in 1 and a slow heart rhythm in 1), none more than 12 hours after arrival, and all 250 patients left hospital alive; no complication after 12 hours in 250 patients is compatible with a true rate of up to 1.5% (editors' calculation). In COCHPA, 2 of the 246 are known to have died (21 of the other 244 could not be followed up), both within 8 hours after arriving in cardiac arrest and neither with pathological evidence of infarction, and no patient developed an arrhythmia needing treatment, heart failure or extension of an infarction in hospital (with 14 infarctions, the authors give a 95% CI of 0% to 21% for late complications). In a records study of 136 cocaine-associated infarctions in 130 patients at 29 US hospitals (1987–1993; entry required cocaine use within 24 hours by history, or a positive urine test), complications were recorded 64 times in 49 patients (36%; the 2008 statement gives 38%), 31 of the 64 were already present on arrival, 5 of the 49 had their first complication more than 12 hours after arrival, and no one died in hospital (0 of 136; 95% CI printed as 0% to 2%, exact upper limit 2.7%, editors' calculation); people who died before reaching hospital could not be included (Hollander et al., 1995b). In the same series, none of the 25 patients given clot-dissolving (thrombolytic) treatment by their clinicians' choice, of 66 eligible by their first electrocardiogram, had bleeding into the brain or bleeding needing transfusion, but with 25 patients a rate of up to about 14% cannot be excluded (exact 95% interval 0 to 13.7%, editors' calculation; printed 0 to 12%); patients treated who turned out not to have an infarction were not included, and with 11 earlier case reports the authors count one fatal bleed into the brain in 36 treated patients (Hollander et al., 1995). Among the 302 lower-risk patients at the Flint hospital in 1998–1999, observed for 9 to 12 hours with troponin I tests on arrival and at 3, 6 and 9 hours (one group without a comparison, not the randomized study the 2008 statement calls it), no one died of a heart cause within 30 days (0 of 302; exact upper 95% limit 1.2%, editors' calculation), 2 died of other causes (a gunshot wound and a heroin overdose), and 4 of the 256 with detailed follow-up had a non-fatal infarction (1.6%; exact 95% CI 0.4% to 4.0%, editors' calculation), all four among people who had continued to use cocaine (Weber et al., 2003). Over about a year after an emergency visit to four of COCHPA's six centres (enrolment 1991–1992), all 203 patients who had left hospital alive were traced, through contacts, charts and the National Death Index (mean 408 days): 6 died (3.0%; exact 95% CI 1.1% to 6.3%, editors' calculation), none of an infarction (3 of complications of HIV disease, 1 of end-stage kidney disease, 1 of sepsis and 1 of cardiac arrest in hospital with heart failure from a cardiomyopathy attributed to alcohol), and 2 had a non-fatal infarction confirmed by CK-MB (1%; exact 0.1% to 3.5%, editors' calculation), counted only from hospital discharge diagnoses that patients reported or charts showed, so further infarctions may have been missed. Of the 130 who answered, 78 said they had kept using cocaine, and they reported chest pain again more often (51 of 68 against 16 of 52); both infarctions and 4 of the deaths were among them and none among the 52 who said they had stopped, an unadjusted difference that was not statistically significant, and the other 2 deaths were in patients whose use was unknown (Hollander et al., 1995c). How often the first electrocardiogram showed ischaemia or infarction in people found to have an infarction differed between studies: 5 of 14 in COCHPA (sensitivity 35.7%, specificity 89.9%), 13 of 15 at the Flint hospital (editors' sum of the 9 consistent with infarction and the 4 ischaemic), 4 of 6 with diagnostic ST elevation in Richmond, and both of the 2 in the 1993 trial. Only the 1993 trial made a comparison, without adjustment: an infarction was diagnosed in 0.7% of the 293 against 2.8% of 2,165 trial patients younger than 45 without recorded cocaine use (P = .033) and 8.6% of all 10,396 others; but the entry ages differed by design (18 or older with suspected cocaine use, 30 or older otherwise), the groups differed in age, sex and smoking, and cocaine use was not screened for uniformly, so this does not show a lower risk with cocaine. These figures describe people who reached US hospitals between 1987 and 1999, mostly young men in cities, many of them smoking crack, mostly tested with CK-MB enzymes, the standard of the time (troponin I only in the 2003 observation protocol); they are not the chance of a heart attack each time a person uses cocaine.
plain: In US studies from the late 1980s and the 1990s of people who went to hospital with chest pain (or similar symptoms) after using cocaine, about 1 to 6 in 100 were having a heart attack; counting only the people kept in hospital, up to about 9 in 100. The share changed with who was included and how a heart attack was tested for: the study that took the widest range of symptoms, and rarely repeated the blood tests in people sent home, found under 1 in 100. Few people died in hospital, and problems mostly came early: at one hospital, among 250 people with chest pain, 7 problems were recorded, none more than 12 hours after arrival, and all went home alive; among 136 heart attacks after cocaine at 29 hospitals, 36 in 100 brought problems such as an irregular heartbeat, about half of the problems were already there on arrival, and no one died in hospital. Among lower-risk people watched for 9 to 12 hours, none died of heart causes within a month; 4 of 256 later had a heart attack, all of whom had kept using cocaine. About a year after a hospital visit, 6 of 203 people had died, none of a heart attack (3 of them of HIV complications), and 2 had had a heart attack and survived; both heart attacks and 4 of the deaths were in people who said they had kept using cocaine, too few to show that continuing was the cause. A first heart tracing (ECG) showed signs in about a third of the heart attacks in one study but in most of them in others. In the one study that also looked at people without recorded cocaine use, heart attacks were less common among those who had used cocaine, but the groups differed in age and in other ways, so this does not show that cocaine changes the risk either way. These were mostly young men in US cities, tested with older blood tests that could miss small heart attacks; the studies do not give anyone's chance of a heart attack each time they use cocaine.
population: Adults who came to US hospital emergency departments with chest pain, or other symptoms suggesting heart ischaemia, after recent cocaine use: six inner-city teaching hospitals in four cities (1991–1992), one hospital in Flint, Michigan (1996–1998 and 1998–1999), one in Richmond, Virginia (1994–1996) and 10 hospitals with urban, suburban and semirural catchment areas (1993); and hospital patients with a confirmed cocaine-associated infarction at 29 US hospitals (1987–1993)
exposure: Recent cocaine use by the patient's report or a positive urine test: use in the previous week reported (COCHPA, self-report; Flint, report or a positive urine screen), recent use acknowledged or a positive screen (Richmond; the 1993 trial, without a stated window), mostly by smoking crack where the route was recorded; in the 29-hospital series, use within 24 hours by history, or a positive urine test
comparator: None for most figures (no patients with the same symptoms who had not used cocaine); in the 1993 trial, an unadjusted comparison with other trial patients without recorded cocaine use; in the 29-hospital thrombolysis report, eligible patients who were not given the treatment
outcome: Acute myocardial infarction as each study defined it (CK-MB above the hospital's limit within 24 hours; WHO criteria with serial CK-MB; CK-MB mass with a relative index and a rise and fall); in-hospital complications and deaths; deaths and non-fatal infarctions within 30 days after a 9-to-12-hour observation with troponin I; major bleeding after thrombolytic treatment
magnitude: Infarction among all patients enrolled: 0.7% (2 of 293; exact 95% CI 0.08–2.4%; WHO criteria; chest pain or other symptoms suggesting ischaemia; 10 US hospitals, 1993); 2.5% of 241 visits (6 infarctions; 6 of 218 patients is 2.8%, editors' calculation; CK-MB mass with relative index; Richmond, 1994–1996); 5.7% (14 of 246 enrolments, some of them repeat visits by the same people; printed 95% CI 2.7–8.7%, exact 3.1–9.4%, editors' calculation; CK-MB above the hospital's limit within 24 hours; six hospitals in four cities, 1991–1992); 6% (15 of 250 admitted under a policy of admitting all; printed 95% CI 3.1–8.9%, abstract 4.1–8.9%, exact 3.4–9.7%, editors' calculation; WHO criteria with serial CK-MB; Flint, 1996–1998). Among patients kept in hospital or tested most fully: 8.6% (COCHPA, admitted), 7.3% (COCHPA, two or more enzyme measurements), 8.7% (6 of 69 admitted, Richmond). High-risk patients admitted directly (Flint, 1998–1999): infarction in 10 of 42. Earlier retrospective series (second-hand): 0% to 31%. In-hospital course: 7 complications in 250 patients, none after 12 hours (upper 95% limit 1.5%, editors' calculation), no deaths (Flint); 2 known deaths in 246 (21 of the other 244 not followed up), both arriving in cardiac arrest without pathological evidence of infarction (COCHPA); confirmed infarction (29 hospitals, 1987–1993): complications recorded 64 times in 49 patients (36%; 38% in the AHA statement), 31 of 64 present on arrival, first complication after 12 hours in 5 of 49, in-hospital deaths 0 of 136 (exact upper limit 2.7%, editors' calculation); no major complication in 25 given thrombolytic treatment (exact 95% CI 0–13.7%, editors' calculation). 30 days after a 9-to-12-hour observation of 302 lower-risk patients (Flint, 1998–1999): cardiovascular deaths 0 (exact upper limit 1.2%), non-fatal infarction in 4 of 256 (1.6%; exact 0.4–4.0%; editors' calculations), all in people who continued to use cocaine. About one year (mean 408 days) after an emergency visit (four COCHPA centres, enrolment 1991–1992): deaths 6 of 203 (3.0%; exact 1.1–6.3%), none from infarction; non-fatal infarction 2 of 203 (1%; printed 95% CI 0–2%, exact 0.1–3.5%; editors' calculations); both infarctions and 4 deaths among the 78 of 130 who said they kept using cocaine, none among the 52 who said they had stopped (death odds ratio 6.3, 0.3–120.3; infarction 3.4, 0.2–72.9; unadjusted). First ECG showing ischaemia or infarction among infarctions: 5 of 14 (COCHPA; sensitivity 35.7%, specificity 89.9%), 13 of 15 (Flint, editors' sum), 4 of 6 with ST elevation (Richmond), 2 of 2 (1993 trial). Unadjusted comparison (1993 trial): infarction 0.7% against 2.8% (Table 2 and abstract; 2.4% in the Results text) in trial patients younger than 45 without recorded cocaine use and 8.6% in all others.

evidence.extracted: Substudy of the ACI-TIPI Clinical Trial, run in 1993 in the emergency departments of 10 public and private, community and tertiary US hospitals with urban, suburban and semirural catchment areas; the trial enrolled all consenting patients aged 30 or older, or 18 or older if recent cocaine use was suspected or reported, who presented with chief complaints of chest, left arm, jaw or epigastric pain or discomfort, shortness of breath, dizziness, palpitations or other symptoms suggestive of acute cardiac ischaemia. Of 10,689 patients, 293 (2.7%) reported recent cocaine use or had a positive toxicology screen (0.3% to 8.3% of patients by hospital in the Results and Discussion; 0.3% to 8.4% in the abstract); they were 75% men and 77% black, mean age 33.5 years, and chest pain was the chief complaint for 87%. Acute myocardial infarction by WHO criteria (at least 2 of: a history of ischaemic-type chest discomfort, changes on serial ECGs, a rise and fall of serum cardiac markers): 2 of 293 (0.7%; 95% CI 0.08% to 2.4% in the abstract, by the exact method the Methods name; 0 to 1.6% in the Results), both with clear ECG evidence of infarction on the presenting ECG; confirmed acute cardiac ischaemia in 6 (2.0%; 95% CI 0.76% to 4.4%), 4 of them unstable angina. Of the 166 discharged from the emergency department, 38 (23%) returned for the 24-hour re-evaluation; of the 127 hospitalized, 42 went to the coronary care unit. Serial CK results were available for 109 of the 127 admitted and more than one CK result for 37 of the 166 discharged; 20 had a raised CK-MB on arrival, of whom 2 had an infarction. The authors say the sevenfold difference in infarction from the two earlier prospective series may be because of their broader inclusion criteria and differences in diagnosing infarction.

evidence.extracted: Unadjusted comparisons within the trial. Against all 10,396 other trial patients, classified as not using cocaine (including use unknown): confirmed infarction 0.7% against 8.6%; mean age 33.5 against 59.3 years; women 25% against 49% (Table 1). Against 2,165 trial patients younger than 45 without recorded cocaine use: infarction 0.7% against 2.8% (difference 2.1 percentage points, 95% CI 0.9 to 3.3; P = .033; the Results text prints this comparison as 0.7% against 2.4%, while Table 2 and the abstract give 2.8%), unstable angina 1.4% against 2.4%, 30-day mortality 0 of 245 against 0.6% of 1,925 (P = .24); mean age 33.5 against 37.5 years, women 25% against 45%, current smoking 87% against 52% (Table 2). The authors say the inclusion criteria (entry at 18 or older for suspected or reported cocaine use, 30 or older otherwise) preclude an age-matched comparison, and that uniform screening for cocaine use was not required at any centre, so screening may have missed patients who had used cocaine, including some who may have had confirmed ischaemia.

evidence.extracted: Medical College of Virginia Hospitals, Richmond, January 1994 to June 1996: all patients who presented to the emergency department with symptoms consistent with myocardial ischaemia after recent cocaine use, acknowledged by the patient or shown by a positive urine drug screen (screening was routine for admitted patients with a history of cocaine use or aged under 50 without known coronary disease). 218 consecutive patients had 245 evaluations; 4 who left against medical advice were excluded, leaving 241 visits. High-risk patients (25) went to the coronary care unit; the others had rest sestamibi perfusion imaging in the emergency department, and low-risk patients with a negative scan were discharged from the emergency department (172 visits not admitted, 69 admitted). Infarction was defined as CK-MB of 8.0 ng/mL or more with a relative index of 4.0 or more and a characteristic rise and fall of cardiac markers, with serial CK and CK-MB sampling in admitted patients. Infarction was documented in 6 of the 69 admitted (8.7%), 2.5% of all patients (the 241 visits); 4 of the 6 had diagnostic ST-segment elevation. Of the 172 not admitted, 39 returned for stress perfusion imaging, all normal, and 115 of the other 133 were known to be alive without cardiac events 30 days after the visit; follow-up was unknown for 18, none of whom appeared in the state death registry. The authors list as limitations that serial marker results were obtained in only a minority of patients and that probably not all patients with cocaine-associated chest pain were included. Editors' calculation: 6 of 218 patients is 2.8%; exact 95% CI 0.9% to 5.3% for 6 of 241.

evidence.extracted: Prospective follow-up of patients enrolled with chest pain after cocaine use reported for the preceding week at four of COCHPA's six centres (Bronx Municipal Hospital Center, New York City Poison Control Center, Highland General Hospital in Oakland and Boston City Hospital; enrolment 30 April 1991 to 29 May 1992): 214 emergency visits by 205 patients; 2 arrived in cardiac arrest and died within 8 hours, leaving 203 followed after leaving hospital or the emergency department, by telephone, letters and charts at 3, 6 and 12 months and one year after enrolment ended, with a National Death Index search for everyone lost to follow-up. Vital status was known for all 203 at a mean of 408 days (SD 117). Six died (one-year actuarial survival 98%, 95% CI 95% to 100%), none from infarction: 3 of complications of HIV disease, 1 of end-stage renal disease with multiorgan failure, 1 of sepsis and 1 of cardiac arrest during a hospitalization for heart failure from a dilated cardiomyopathy attributed to alcohol (the one death the authors count as cardiovascular). Two had a non-fatal infarction (1%; printed 95% CI 0% to 2%), both confirmed by CK-MB; a later infarction was counted when patients reported, or charts showed, a hospitalization with a discharge diagnosis of infarction, patients refused to return for repeat ECGs, and the authors cannot exclude that further non-fatal infarctions went undiagnosed. Editors' calculations: exact 95% CIs 1.1% to 6.3% for 6 of 203 and 0.1% to 3.5% for 2 of 203. Editors' comparison: the parent study lists 99, 13, 57 and 45 enrolments at these four centres (Hollander et al., 1994, Appendix A, p. 339), 214 in all, the number of visits here, so the 246 that COCHPA calls patients were enrolments, some of them repeat visits by the same people.

evidence.extracted: Recurrent chest pain and continued cocaine use were asked about when patients could be contacted directly; relatives or colleagues who were contacted were not asked about drug use (information on it that they volunteered was recorded) and were not always aware of recurrent chest pain, and no urine was tested at follow-up. Of 130 patients who answered, 78 said they had kept using cocaine (60%; 95% CI 52% to 68%); recurrent chest pain was reported by 74 of 136 (54%; 46% to 63%), by 51 of 68 who kept using against 16 of 52 who said they had stopped (odds ratio 6.5, 2.9 to 14.4). The authors state that the sample size prohibits firm conclusions about the effect of continued use, and that recurrent chest pain, infarction and cocaine use may all be underestimated. Editors' calculation: Fisher's exact P = 0.15 for death and 0.52 for infarction.

risk_of_bias.note: The studies read in full (JBI prevalence checklist: COCHPA, Weber et al. 2000 and 2003 and the 1993 trial moderate; Kontos et al. and the 29-hospital complication report high; cards sc_hollander_1994, sc_weber_2000, sc_weber_2003, sc_feldman_2000, sc_kontos_1999, sc_hollander_1995b) found patients through records coded for cocaine or drug use, through investigators' enrolment or through clinicians' questioning, tested urine selectively, and measured enzymes completely mainly in admitted patients (COCHPA: enzymes in 215 of 246, repeated in 151; the 1993 trial: more than one CK for 37 of 166 sent home; Richmond: serial markers only in the 69 admitted visits of 241), which can move the share in either direction; the 29-hospital thrombolysis report compares clinicians' treatment choices without adjustment (card sc_hollander_1995: ROBINS-I serious), which matters only for that observation. The one-year follow-up (card sc_hollander_1995c) traced vital status for all 203 patients but counted later infarctions only from reported or charted admissions (a minimum), and its comparison by self-reported continued use is crude (ROBINS-E very high), so it is reported as counts only.

inconsistency.note: Shares among all patients enrolled range from 0.7% to 6% (to 8.7% among admitted patients). The authors of the 1993 trial suggest their sevenfold lower figure may come from broader inclusion (symptoms other than chest pain) and different criteria (WHO criteria need a rise and fall of markers, rarely measurable in patients sent home), and COCHPA's and Kontos et al.'s own figures rise among admitted or fully tested patients; these explanations fit, but they were not tested across studies.

indirectness.note: CK-MB and WHO criteria of 1987–1999 rather than today's troponin-based definitions (troponin I only in the 2003 observation protocol); US hospitals, mostly urban; mostly young men, many smoking crack; the 29-hospital series concerns patients with a confirmed infarction, not all patients with chest pain.

imprecision.note: Each study's share has a usable exact interval (for example 3.4% to 9.7% for 15 of 250 and 0.08% to 2.4% for 2 of 293); the thrombolysis observation (0 of 25), the 30-day non-fatal infarctions (4 of 256) and the one-year deaths and non-fatal infarctions (6 and 2 of 203) are imprecise and are reported with their intervals rather than rated down.

grade.reasoning: Shares of patients with an infarction are descriptive (relation 'describes', METHODS §6.1, §6.3): they start low and are not upgraded. Down one each for risk of bias, inconsistency and indirectness, which is below the floor: very low. All the emergency-department studies behind the figures are now read in full (Hollander et al., 1994, 1995, 1995b, 1995c; Kontos et al., 1999; Weber et al., 2000, 2003; Feldman et al., 2000); the AHA statement (McCord et al., 2008) is cited only for its summary range, and it misdescribes the 2003 observation study as randomized. Overlap, counted once: J. E. Hollander led COCHPA, its one-year follow-up (the same patients at four of its six centres) and the 29-hospital series, is senior author of both Flint studies and was on the AHA writing group; J. A. Feldman and S. S. Fish ran COCHPA's Boston site and wrote the 1993-trial analysis; Kontos et al. (Richmond) are a separate team. Status replicated: studies by independent teams (COCHPA and the Flint series; Kontos et al.) agree that a small minority of these patients had an infarction, and the 1993 trial found fewer; the spread is part of the claim and is rated under inconsistency. The figures describe people who reached hospital, not the risk of infarction per occasion of cocaine use; the only comparison with patients without recorded cocaine use (the 1993 trial) is unadjusted and confounded by its entry rules. Papers of 12 November (evening): the one-year follow-up (Hollander et al., 1995c) adds counts of later deaths and infarctions in the same cohort as COCHPA, not independent evidence, and does not bear on how often chest pain after cocaine is an infarction, so the rating is unchanged; it also shows that COCHPA's 246 were enrolments, some of them repeat visits by the same people. Its card (sc_hollander_1995c) is first-pass, and its two anchors stay ai-located until a second reader checks them.
