statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether a beta-blocker given in hospital to people with chest pain after cocaine use makes the narrowing of the heart's arteries, heart attacks or deaths more likely: the only experimental evidence is two small laboratory studies of artery size and blood flow (one of them randomized), and the clinical evidence is hospital records in which doctors chose whom to treat. That cocaine itself narrows the coronary arteries and reduces blood flow to the heart muscle for a time was shown in a randomized, double-blind laboratory study of 30 patients undergoing cardiac catheterization for chest pain, none with a history of cocaine use (Dallas, published 1990): in the 15 given intranasal cocaine 2 mg/kg (110 to 210 mg, a study condition the authors describe as one half to two thirds of the amount used to numb the nose and throat), measured 15 minutes later against their own baseline, systolic blood pressure rose by 11 mm Hg (95% CI 5 to 16), coronary sinus blood flow fell by 17 mL/min (5 to 29) and coronary vascular resistance rose, and six measured artery segments narrowed by 0.10 to 0.25 mm (about 6% to 10%, editors' calculation), significantly in four, while nothing changed in the 15 given intranasal saline (no test between the two groups is reported); no one had chest pain or electrocardiographic signs of ischaemia after cocaine alone (Lange et al., 1990). In a second study by the same group, in which all 15 patients received the same dose and none was given a placebo, the area of disease-free artery segments fell by about 9% and 17% in its two arms (editors' calculation from the means; Boehrer et al., 1993). In the 1990 study, 10 of the patients given cocaine then received the beta-blocker propranolol infused directly into the left coronary artery (2 mg over 5 minutes): coronary sinus flow fell further, from 120 to 100 mL/min (change from the post-cocaine value −20 mL/min, 95% CI −42 to −1, P = 0.050), and resistance rose further (+0.16 mm Hg/mL per min, −0.02 to 0.33, P = 0.074), although the abstract reports P < 0.05 for both; flow fell and resistance rose in all 10, but the average diameters of the six artery segments did not change significantly (P 0.19 to 1.00), and the authors could not exclude that the drug lowered flow by reducing the heart's contractility. Nothing changed further in 5 patients given an intracoronary saline infusion after cocaine, nothing changed in 5 given propranolol after intranasal saline, and the randomized comparison between the two groups given cocaine was not tested. In 5 of the 10 an artery segment narrowed by more than 10%, and in one a coronary artery closed completely, with ischaemic symptoms and ST-segment elevation, which resolved after sublingual nitroglycerin without a rise in creatine kinase (Lange et al., 1990). In the 1993 study, intravenous labetalol (0.25 mg/kg), which blocks alpha as well as beta receptors, given to 9 such patients after cocaine lowered mean arterial pressure from 117 to 110 mm Hg but left the narrowed artery area unchanged (3.47 to 3.37 mm²); heart rate did not change at any point, so beta-blockade was not shown, allocation to labetalol or to saline (6 patients) was not described as randomized, and the two groups differed at baseline (Boehrer et al., 1993). Resting on these two studies (30 and 15 patients enrolled, of whom 10 and 9 received the blocker after cocaine; editors' count), on case reports and on animal experiments in which beta-blockers reduced coronary blood flow and increased seizures and deaths, the 2008 American Heart Association statement recommends that beta-blockers be avoided in the acute setting (Class III, Level of Evidence C, which it defines as consensus opinion of experts, case studies or standard of care), noting that no randomized placebo-controlled trial of treatment for cocaine-associated infarction had been reported and that deaths from cocaine-associated infarction are very low, which alters the balance of risk and benefit; at discharge it reserves long-term beta-blockers for people with a documented infarction, a weakened left ventricle or ventricular arrhythmias, decided individually after counselling about the interaction between renewed cocaine use and beta-blockade (McCord et al., 2008). Hospital records, all retrospective and non-randomized, cover the clinical outcomes, and in all of them doctors chose whom to treat. At two hospitals affiliated with one university (three of the five authors were at Saint Louis University), 164 of 376 patients (44%) with chest pain, cocaine use reported within 24 hours and a cocaine-positive urine screen in 2000–2007 were given a beta-blocker within 24 hours (metoprolol 74, labetalol 44, carvedilol 43, atenolol 3, so 87 received a drug that also blocks alpha receptors); they were older and had more hypertension and coronary disease, which the propensity score included, and received more aspirin, nitrates and other cardiac drugs, which it did not. In-hospital myocardial infarction, stroke, ventricular arrhythmia or death occurred in 16% of them and 12% of the others (odds ratio adjusted for propensity-score quintile 1.37, 95% CI 0.64 to 2.93); myocardial infarction in 5% against 2% (1.67, 0.44 to 6.35), although the troponin values reported do not fit the stated definition, so how infarction was counted is unclear; death in 3% against 6% (0.66, 0.14 to 3.04); the odds ratio was 1.83 (0.79 to 4.24) for beta-1-selective drugs and 0.90 (0.33 to 2.42) for carvedilol or labetalol, not tested against each other (Fanari et al., 2014). At San Francisco General Hospital in 2001–2006, 151 of 328 patients admitted with chest pain and a cocaine-positive urine test through the emergency department were given a beta-blocker there (the first dose mostly intravenous metoprolol), at the doctors' discretion: troponin in the infarction range was found in 15 of them (10%) against 18 of 177 (10%), and 2 against 3 died in hospital (unadjusted); vasopressors were needed by 1 (1%) against 12 (7%), and the authors cannot exclude that the treated patients were healthier in ways not measured; over a median 972 days, death, the primary outcome, was not associated with a beta-blocker in the emergency department (hazard ratio 0.97, 0.53 to 1.79), and a lower adjusted risk of cardiovascular death with discharge on a beta-blocker (0.29, 0.09 to 0.98; 19 deaths) was a secondary result that the authors call likely overinflated (Rangel et al., 2010). At a Bronx municipal hospital in 2000–2005, among 310 admissions with a cocaine-positive urine test and troponin measured (about half for chest pain), infarction followed a beta-blocker in 2 of 33 admissions against 72 of 277 (unadjusted odds ratio 0.17, 0.04 to 0.80; adjusted 0.06, 0.01 to 0.61); but an infarction counted against the beta-blocker only if it came after the drug and before a documented troponin rise, whereas every infarction during the admission counted in the comparison group, which also took in the admissions given a beta-blocker after their infarction, a comparison that favours the beta-blocker group (editors' reading), and the paper's figure, unlike its text, labels 31 of the 33 treated admissions as given the drug after an infarction; in-hospital deaths were 1 of 60 against 13 of 288 (adjusted 0.22, 0.02 to 2.41), the one death after a beta-blocker following thrombolysis for an infarction that came before the drug (Dattilo et al., 2008). Replying to a letter, two of its authors said that the figure did not show their data correctly, that 55 of the 60 admissions given a beta-blocker had troponin measured, and that those given it after their infarction were counted, with those infarctions, in the comparison group (22 admissions, editors' calculation from the 33 given it before any infarction): against the 255 admissions never given a beta-blocker, infarction was 2 of 33 against 50 of 255 (crude risk ratio 0.31, 95% CI 0.08 to 1.21, against 0.23, 0.06 to 0.91, for the published groups; editors' calculation), with follow-up still starting at the drug in one group and at admission in the other (Fung et al., 2008). A second letter asked how blood pressure responded, and the authors replied that it had not been consistently recorded after the drug (Mariani, 2008). Two editorials printed with this cohort drew opposite conclusions without data of their own: one argued that the evidence still speaks against beta-blockers after cocaine and that a trial would be premature and dangerous (Hoffman, 2008); the other, that the caution rests on uncontrolled observations, beginning with a 1985 report of one patient, on surrogate end points and on animal models, and that beta-blockers should not be withheld from patients with an acute coronary syndrome and a positive urine test who are not acutely intoxicated (Freeman & Feldman, 2008). At a Detroit emergency department in 2004–2005, among 364 people with chest pain, cocaine use in the previous 24 hours and a cocaine-positive urine test, those already taking a beta-blocker at home when they arrived had a raised troponin (above 0.02 ng/mL) more often (14 of 100, against 4.4% of the others), and a later troponin rise was reported in 9 of 39 patients whose beta-blocker was continued in hospital (23.3% for continuing or starting one, against 10.7% of other admitted patients, a group whose size is not given); both comparisons were unadjusted, and patients with a raised troponin far more often had a history of coronary disease (51.9% against 5.1%) (Mohamad et al., 2008). At two Houston hospitals in 1998–2011, troponin rose in 22 of 162 patients (13.6%) given a beta-blocker at some time during admission against 20 of 216 (9.3%) not given one (unadjusted, P = .191), with the timing of the drug relative to the troponin rise not determined, about twice the rates of hypertension and coronary disease among the treated, and the counts printed differently in the abstract and text (Ibrahim et al., 2013). At Metropolitan Hospital Center in New York City in 2006–2009, of 378 patients admitted with chest pain finally diagnosed as cocaine-induced and a cocaine-positive urine test, 26 had been given one dose of a beta-blocker in the emergency department while the pain continued (metoprolol in 18, by mouth in 13; labetalol, carvedilol, atenolol or propranolol in 2 each), the patients with higher blood pressure and heart rate being more likely to receive one; they were compared with 32 patients not given one while in pain, described as paired by age, sex, race and hypertension but chosen in a way the paper does not describe, and nothing is reported on the other 320 (editors' arithmetic). No one in either group died or had a recorded cardiac complication (cardiac complications not defined; for 0 of 26, an exact 95% upper limit of 13.2%, editors' calculation); blood pressure and heart rate did not differ significantly in any window up to 6 hours (mean systolic 147.8 against 135.5 in the first hour and 126.7 against 130.1 at 3 to 6 hours, units not printed), although the text reports lower values with the beta-blocker at 6 and 12 hours, which no table shows; troponin I was positive in 7 of 26 against 7 of 32 at 0 to 3 hours, 4 against 5 at 3 to 6 hours and 3 against 5 at 6 to 12 hours, with no threshold given, no count of patients positive at any time and no result called an infarction, in a cohort defined by its final diagnosis; and the treated patients stayed longer (4.6 against 2.65 days, P = 0.04), which the authors put down, without data, to unrelated causes (Espana Schmidt et al., 2015). Three meta-analyses pooled unadjusted counts from these cohorts, so none is independent of them or of the others. Pham et al. (2018) pooled the first five (1756 patients; 1794 in its abstract; it does not cite Espana Schmidt et al.'s cohort): non-fatal infarction in 94 of 610 patients (15.4%) given a beta-blocker and 162 of 1146 (14.1%) not given one (odds ratio 1.36, 0.68 to 2.74; I² 71%) and death in 6 of 348 (1.7%) against 22 of 666 (3.3%) (0.68, 0.26 to 1.79; three cohorts). Shin et al. (2019) pooled all six and two others (eight cohorts, 2,048 patients, searched to June 2018): relative risks of 1.24 (0.74 to 2.06; I² 63%) for in-hospital infarction or myocardial necrosis, 0.59 (0.24 to 1.47) for in-hospital death, 0.79 (0.44 to 1.41) for death over a mean of 2.6 years and 0.96 (0.40 to 2.33) for later infarction. Lo et al. (2019) pooled four of the first five (not Mohamad et al.'s, whose data it judged insufficient) and Espana Schmidt et al.'s (five cohorts, 1,447 patients, searched to July 2018): risk ratios of 1.08 (0.61 to 1.91; I² 51%) for infarction and, from the four cohorts with a row in its death analysis (three estimable; 1,072 patients, Ibrahim et al.'s cohort having none), 0.75 (0.46 to 1.24) for death, which it calls in-hospital although 80.6% of that analysis's weight is Rangel et al.'s deaths over a median of 972 days (18 of 151 against 27 of 177) rather than its in-hospital deaths (2 against 3); it reported no assessment of the cohorts' risk of bias or of publication bias, and its statements that labetalol and metoprolol appear safe rest on no analysis by drug. In Pham et al.'s and Shin et al.'s analyses, the only single cohorts with significant results point in opposite directions and are the two comparisons most open to bias (Dattilo et al.'s and Mohamad et al.'s); without them the other in-hospital infarction estimates agree (relative risk 1.17, 0.86 to 1.61, I² 0%; editors' calculation from Shin et al.'s counts), as they do in Lo et al.'s without Dattilo et al.'s (1.29, 0.88 to 1.88, I² 0%; editors' calculation from Lo et al.'s counts), and still do when Espana Schmidt et al.'s troponin rows are also left out (1.31, 0.85 to 2.03, I² 6%, and 1.30, 0.85 to 2.00, I² 4%; editors' calculations). All three reviews entered Fanari et al.'s percentages as event counts and Dattilo et al.'s deaths over the denominators of its infarction analysis; Pham et al. entered as Rangel et al.'s infarctions the sum of its any-positive-troponin and infarction-range counts (51 and 55 instead of 15 and 18), and Shin et al. gave Mohamad et al.'s comparison group as 254 instead of 264 and, for long-term death, used Rangel et al.'s emergency-department comparison rather than its discharge comparison. The two reviews that pooled Espana Schmidt et al.'s cohort entered its troponin results as infarctions: Lo et al. its first window (7 of 26 against 7 of 32, 20.5% of the analysis's weight), while describing the study as a cohort of 378 that found significantly lower blood pressure with a beta-blocker, which its tables do not show; Shin et al. the sums of its three windows, as infarction or necrosis (14 of 26 against 17 of 32, 23.2% of the weight, the most of any cohort), which counts a patient positive in more than one window more than once, with the drug's timing given as during admission or at discharge although the paper describes one emergency-department dose, stopped once cocaine metabolites were found in the urine. With the in-hospital entries corrected no pooled estimate becomes significant (editors' calculations, with a method that reproduces the printed results exactly from the printed counts: infarction 1.32, 0.62 to 2.80, and death 0.51, 0.22 to 1.17, in Pham et al.'s analyses; in-hospital infarction 1.26, 0.76 to 2.09, and death 0.48, 0.22 to 1.04, in Shin et al.'s; infarction 1.11, 0.64 to 1.93, and death with Rangel et al.'s in-hospital deaths 0.52, 0.23 to 1.16, in Lo et al.'s), nor without Espana Schmidt et al.'s troponin rows, which report no infarctions (in-hospital infarction 1.30, 0.65 to 2.57, in Shin et al.'s analysis and 1.03, 0.48 to 2.18, in Lo et al.'s; 1.32, 0.68 to 2.57, and 1.06, 0.52 to 2.17, with the other entries also corrected; editors' calculations). Pham et al.'s text attributes the one significant increase in infarction to the cohort that found a significant decrease, and it describes the two laboratory studies as giving 45 people intravenous beta-blockers (Pham et al., 2018). The laboratory studies measured artery size and blood flow for minutes after one moderate dose in people with no history of cocaine use, with propranolol infused into a coronary artery rather than given by vein or by mouth; the hospital records could not tell whether cocaine was still active when the drug was given (urine screens stay positive for 2 to 3 days), counted the drug over different windows (taken at home before arrival, before an infarction, in the emergency department, within 24 hours, at any time in hospital, at discharge), defined infarction by troponin thresholds from 0.02 to 1.5 ng/mL (one gave no threshold and counted no infarctions), mixed drugs with and without alpha-blocking action, and had too few events to exclude either harm or benefit. No randomized trial of beta-blockers in people with chest pain after cocaine had been reported by June 2018 (Shin et al., 2019), and a search to July 2018 found no trial with clinical outcomes (Lo et al., 2019).
plain: In a hospital laboratory, one moderate dose of cocaine put into the nose of heart patients with no history of cocaine use narrowed their heart arteries a little and cut blood flow to the heart muscle for a time; a dummy dose did nothing. When 10 of them were then given the beta-blocker propranolol (beta-blockers are common heart and blood-pressure medicines) straight into a heart artery, blood flow fell further in all 10, and in one person an artery closed until doctors gave nitroglycerin; this did not happen with a dummy infusion, or with propranolol given without cocaine, though on average the arteries did not narrow further. Labetalol, which blocks alpha as well as beta receptors, lowered blood pressure in 9 such patients but did not widen their narrowed arteries. Mainly on these small studies, the American Heart Association advised in 2008 against beta-blockers soon after cocaine use, grading this as expert opinion. Hospital records have not clearly shown this harm: in eight studies of about 2,000 patients with chest pain and cocaine in their urine, pooled in three overlapping reviews, heart attacks and deaths were not clearly more or less common in those given a beta-blocker. But doctors chose who got it, nobody knew whether the cocaine was still active, the only two studies that found a clear difference (one each way) counted in ways that bias their results, and all three reviews copied some numbers wrongly (correcting them does not change their results). In one of those studies, from a New York hospital, none of the 26 people given a beta-blocker in the emergency department and none of the 32 people compared with them died or had a recorded heart complication; two reviews counted its blood-test results as heart attacks or heart damage, and one called it a study of 378 people, though it compared 58. The authors of the study that found fewer heart attacks later confirmed that it counted heart attacks that came before the drug in the comparison group. Two editorials printed with that study drew opposite conclusions from the same evidence: one called a trial dangerous, the other said research, not opinion, should decide. No trial has tested beta-blockers in people with chest pain after cocaine, so whether they make things worse is not known. See the contested question.
population: Patients undergoing cardiac catheterization for chest pain with no history of cocaine use (two laboratory studies by one Dallas group: 30 and 15 patients); patients with chest pain (in one cohort, any admission to monitored medical units) and a cocaine-positive urine test at US hospitals in the Bronx, Detroit, San Francisco and Houston, at Metropolitan Hospital Center in New York City (26 treated and 32 selected comparison patients of 378 admitted with a final diagnosis of cocaine-induced chest pain) and at two hospitals affiliated with one university three of whose five authors were at Saint Louis University (six retrospective cohorts, admissions 1998–2011, each read in full), pooled, with two further cohorts, in three meta-analyses (Pham et al., 2018: five of the six; Lo et al., 2019: four of those five and the Metropolitan Hospital cohort; Shin et al., 2019: all six and two further)
exposure: In the laboratory, intranasal cocaine 2 mg/kg (study condition) followed by propranolol infused into the left coronary artery (2 mg) or intravenous labetalol (0.25 mg/kg); in hospitals, beta-blockers given in routine care and counted differently by each cohort: already taken at home before arrival (Mohamad et al.), given before any troponin rise (Dattilo et al.), given in the emergency department (Rangel et al.; one dose while chest pain continued in Espana Schmidt et al.), given at any time during admission (Ibrahim et al.), given within 24 hours (Fanari et al.), or prescribed at discharge (long-term analyses); mostly metoprolol, with labetalol, carvedilol, atenolol and propranolol
comparator: In the laboratory, intranasal saline, a saline infusion after cocaine, and propranolol after intranasal saline; in hospitals, patients with a cocaine-positive urine test not given a beta-blocker as each cohort defined it (in one cohort the comparison group also included admissions given a beta-blocker after their infarction; in another it was 32 patients described as paired by age, sex, race and hypertension and chosen in a way not described)
outcome: Coronary blood flow, coronary vascular resistance and artery size (laboratory); in-hospital myocardial infarction or troponin rise (thresholds from 0.02 to 1.5 ng/mL; in one cohort a positive troponin with no stated threshold, and cardiac complications not defined), stroke, ventricular arrhythmia and death, and death and infarction over 1 to 4 years (hospital records)
magnitude: Not estimable as an effect of beta-blockers on clinical outcomes. Laboratory, change from each group's own baseline (n = 15 each; no between-group test reported): cocaine, coronary sinus flow −17 mL/min (95% CI −29 to −5), resistance +0.18 mm Hg/mL per min (0.13 to 0.24), artery segments −0.10 to −0.25 mm (about 6% to 10%, editors' calculation; 4 of 6 segments significant); saline, no change. Intracoronary propranolol after cocaine (n = 10), change from the post-cocaine value: flow −20 mL/min (−42 to −1; P = 0.050), resistance +0.16 (−0.02 to 0.33; P = 0.074), segment diameters unchanged (P 0.19 to 1.00); complete occlusion in 1 of 10. Intravenous labetalol after cocaine (n = 9): mean arterial pressure 117 to 110 mm Hg; artery area 3.47 to 3.37 mm² (unchanged). Hospital cohorts, all non-randomized: Fanari et al. (376 patients) composite in-hospital outcome 16% against 12%, adjusted odds ratio 1.37 (0.64 to 2.93); infarction 5% against 2%, 1.67 (0.44 to 6.35); death 3% against 6%, 0.66 (0.14 to 3.04). Rangel et al. (331) troponin in the infarction range 15 of 151 against 18 of 177 (unadjusted); death over a median 972 days, hazard ratio 0.97 (0.53 to 1.79). Dattilo et al. (310 admissions) infarction 2 of 33 against 72 of 277, adjusted odds ratio 0.06 (0.01 to 0.61), with events counted from different starting points; against the 255 admissions never given a beta-blocker (from the authors' reply), 2 of 33 against 50 of 255, crude risk ratio 0.31 (0.08 to 1.21; editors' calculation). Mohamad et al. (364) raised troponin with a beta-blocker already taken at home 14 of 100 against 4.4% (unadjusted). Ibrahim et al. (378) troponin rise 22 of 162 against 20 of 216 (unadjusted). Espana Schmidt et al. (58 compared of 378) deaths and recorded cardiac complications 0 of 26 against 0 of 32 (exact 95% upper limit for the treated group 13.2%, editors' calculation); troponin I positive (no threshold stated) 7 of 26 against 7 of 32 at 0 to 3 hours, 4 against 5 at 3 to 6 hours, 3 against 5 at 6 to 12 hours; no significant blood-pressure or heart-rate difference up to 6 hours; stay 4.6 against 2.65 days (P = 0.04). Meta-analyses of these cohorts: Pham et al. (5 cohorts, 1756 patients) non-fatal infarction odds ratio 1.36 (0.68 to 2.74), I² 71%; death 0.68 (0.26 to 1.79), I² 0%. Shin et al. (8 cohorts, 2,048 patients) in-hospital infarction or necrosis relative risk 1.24 (0.74 to 2.06), I² 63% (Espana Schmidt et al.'s three troponin windows summed, 14 of 26 against 17 of 32, weight 23.2%); in-hospital death 0.59 (0.24 to 1.47); long-term death 0.79 (0.44 to 1.41); long-term infarction 0.96 (0.40 to 2.33). evidence.extracted: An editorial (Toxicology/Editorial) by one author (Department of Emergency Medicine, New York University School of Medicine, and New York City Poison Center), printed with Dattilo et al. (2008), with no data of its own. He argues that the catheterization studies (cocaine-induced coronary constriction worsened by propranolol, relieved by phentolamine and essentially unaffected by labetalol), with animal experiments, provided sufficient evidence for the American Heart Association International Liaison Committee on Resuscitation to caution against routine beta-blockers in patients with cocaine use and chest pain; that Dattilo et al.'s cohort is hard to compare with prospective chest-pain cohorts, since fewer than half its patients had chest pain and exposure was a positive urine test, which can stay positive 2 to 3 days after intermittent use and up to 2 weeks in chronic use at the cut-off chosen, whereas nearly 90% of documented cocaine-associated infarctions present within 24 hours of last use; that it is difficult to suggest a cardiovascular benefit when only 5% to 6% of these patients have an infarction, those who do have an in-hospital mortality approaching zero, and those in whom infarction is ruled out survive well even if they keep using cocaine; and that, although actual cases of harm are rarely reported, the preponderance of evidence still speaks against beta-blockers in this setting, and the call for a prospective trial seems to him not only premature but quite dangerous. Editors' observations: of the three catheterization studies he calls compelling, only the propranolol study (Lange et al., 1990) tested a beta-blocker with a worse result; 6 of his 31 references name him as an author, among them three of the four prognosis studies he cites (references 19, 20 and 22, not 21); he does not discuss how Dattilo et al. formed their comparison groups. The author declares no relationships related to the subject.

evidence.extracted: An editorial (Toxicology/Editorial) by two physicians (University of Vermont College of Medicine; Boston University School of Medicine), printed with Dattilo et al. (2008), with no data of its own. They argue that both premises of withholding beta-blockers after cocaine, that the chest pain is mainly coronary spasm and that beta-blockers can worsen spasm and cocaine's haemodynamic effects through unopposed alpha stimulation, lack rigorous investigation and rest mainly on uncontrolled observations: the unopposed-alpha idea began with a 1985 report of one patient whose blood pressure rose from 170/118 to 180/140 mm Hg after propranolol, and its other support is catheterization studies, a 7-patient esmolol series and animal models, with blood pressure and coronary constriction as end points of uncertain clinical relevance; they add that beta-blockers are of established benefit in other conditions with high catecholamine levels (heart failure, subarachnoid haemorrhage, the perioperative period). They call Dattilo et al.'s results hypothesis-generating (record abstractors not shown to be blinded; a positive urine test does not show that a patient was intoxicated at presentation; unmeasured confounding), argue against rejecting a trial as dangerous, and conclude that there is no support for withholding beta-blockers from patients with an acute coronary syndrome and a positive urine test who are not acutely intoxicated, while for acute intoxication the answer should come from research and evidence, not opinion. Editors' observations: they describe Dattilo et al.'s multivariable, propensity-score and sensitivity analyses as showing a significant reduction in in-hospital mortality, which holds only for Dattilo et al.'s first-admission sensitivity model (odds ratio 0.01, 0.00 to 0.33; 12 deaths in 296 patients; Dattilo et al., 2008, Results › Sensitivity Analyses and Table 4, p. 123), not for the full-cohort estimate (0.22, 0.02 to 2.41; anchor 22); and they describe the animal evidence as rodent or porcine although one of the three studies they cite was in nonhuman primates (ref 37, p. 134). The authors declare no relationships related to the subject.

risk_of_bias.note: Hospital records, the only clinical evidence: doctors chose whom to treat in every cohort. Three of the six cohorts read in full are at critical risk of bias: infarctions counted from different starting points in the treated and untreated groups (card sc_dattilo_2008; confirmed in the authors' reply to a letter, card sc_fung_2008), beta-blockers taken before arrival compared without adjustment (card sc_mohamad_2008), and an unadjusted comparison with the timing of the drug unknown (card sc_ibrahim_2013) (ROBINS-I critical; first-pass cards whose key points the adjudicator checked in the PDFs); the other three are at serious risk (cards sc_fanari_2014 and sc_rangel_2010: ROBINS-I serious; co-treatment not adjusted for, unadjusted in-hospital comparisons, the drug counted over the first 24 hours while events were counted over the whole stay; card sc_espana_schmidt_2015, a first-pass card whose key points the claim writer checked in the PDF: ROBINS-I serious; 26 treated patients compared without adjustment with 32 chosen in a way not described, in a cohort defined by its final diagnosis, with outcomes undefined and no stated starting time for the comparison group). All three meta-analyses pooled unadjusted counts with misentered rows (cards sc_pham_2018, sc_shin_2019 and sc_lo_2019: AMSTAR 2 critically low; Lo et al.'s death analysis is mostly long-term deaths; Lo et al. and Shin et al. entered Espana Schmidt et al.'s troponin results as infarctions). Laboratory: the propranolol study's conclusion rests on within-person changes rather than the randomized comparison, with the abstract overstating its tests (card sc_lange_1990: RoB 2 high); the labetalol study was neither randomized nor reported as blinded (card sc_boehrer_1993: ROBINS-I serious). Two levels, because most of the pooled weight comes from comparisons at serious or critical risk of bias whose remaining biases could change the estimates materially.

inconsistency.note: Single-study estimates for in-hospital infarction run from benefit to harm (relative risks 0.23 to 3.23, I² 63%; odds ratios 0.18 to 3.30 as entered, I² 71%), but the only two significant results, in opposite directions, come from the two comparisons most open to bias (Dattilo et al.: infarctions before the drug counted against the untreated; Mohamad et al.: beta-blockers taken before arrival), and without them the remaining estimates agree (relative risk 1.17, 0.86 to 1.61, I² 0%; editors' calculation from Shin et al.'s counts; 1.31, 0.85 to 2.03, I² 6%, if Espana Schmidt et al.'s summed troponin results, which are not infarctions, are also left out); in Lo et al.'s review, which left out Mohamad et al.'s cohort (I² 51%), the estimates without Dattilo et al.'s agree (1.29, 0.88 to 1.88, I² 0%; editors' calculation; 1.30, 0.85 to 2.00, I² 4%, without Espana Schmidt et al.'s troponin row as well). The spread is therefore counted under risk of bias and not again here (METHODS §6.3). That the laboratory mechanism and the hospital outcomes point different ways is a difference of question and outcome, counted under indirectness and in the contested status.

indirectness.note: Laboratory: cardiac patients with no history of cocaine use, one moderate intranasal dose, propranolol infused into a coronary artery, and artery size and flow rather than clinical events. Hospital: whether cocaine was still active when the drug was given is unknown (urine screens positive for 2 to 3 days); the exposure was counted over different windows (taken at home before arrival, before an infarction, in the emergency department, within 24 hours, at any time in hospital, at discharge); infarction was defined by troponin thresholds from 0.02 to 1.5 ng/mL, and one cohort reported positive troponin results with no threshold and no infarctions (Espana Schmidt et al.); and the drugs mixed beta-1-selective agents with agents that also block alpha receptors.

imprecision.note: Intervals include both appreciable harm and appreciable benefit (pooled in-hospital infarction 0.74 to 2.06, 0.68 to 2.74 and 0.61 to 1.91; pooled in-hospital death 0.24 to 1.47 and 0.26 to 1.79, from 30 and 28 deaths, and 0.23 to 1.16 in Lo et al.'s analysis with in-hospital counts, editors' calculation; composite outcome in the cohort with a propensity-adjusted estimate 0.64 to 2.93; in the Metropolitan Hospital cohort, no events among 26 treated patients, compatible with a risk of up to 13.2%, editors' exact calculation).

publication_bias.note: Not assessable: Egger's tests on three to six studies (P = 0.580 for in-hospital infarction, six studies) and a funnel plot of five studies cannot show asymmetry, as Shin et al. (2019) say of their own tests; Lo et al. (2019) did not assess it.

grade.reasoning: The clinical question, whether a beta-blocker given in hospital after cocaine changes outcomes, has only non-randomized evidence, which starts low; down two levels for risk of bias, one for indirectness and one for imprecision, which is below the floor: very low. Inconsistency is not rated down separately: the single cohorts point both ways, but the two significant results come from the two comparisons most open to bias and the others agree, so the spread is counted once, under risk of bias (METHODS §6.3). A strict reading that started from the randomized laboratory study would reach the same rating (high, down for risk of bias, two levels for the indirectness of a surrogate outcome in patients with no history of cocaine use given an intracoronary drug, and down for imprecision with 10 treated patients). Counted once: the six cohorts read in full are inside the meta-analyses (Pham et al., 2018, pooled five of them, all but Espana Schmidt et al.'s; Shin et al., 2019, all six and two others; Lo et al., 2019, four of the other five and Espana Schmidt et al.'s), so the single cohorts and the three pooled estimates are not independent support for one another; the two laboratory studies come from one Dallas group and the AHA statement rests on them; one author of the AHA statement (H. Jneid) is also an author of Pham et al. (2018). That cocaine itself narrows the coronary arteries and lowers coronary flow in the minutes after use comes from a randomized, placebo-controlled study (changes within the cocaine group, none within the saline group, no test between them), but in 15 patients with no history of cocaine use given one dose; it is reported as the background to the contested question, not as a separately rated claim. Status contested: a mechanism seen in the laboratory and a professional recommendation point to harm, while the hospital records do not clearly show it, and both rest on weak evidence, so the six-part debate box applies (METHODS §7). Papers of 12 November (evening), read in full: the third meta-analysis (Lo et al., 2019; card sc_lo_2019, AMSTAR 2 critically low) pools largely the same cohorts and also finds no significant difference, so it adds no independent evidence; the two editorials printed with Dattilo et al. (Freeman & Feldman, 2008; Hoffman, 2008) report no data and read the same evidence in opposite ways, which the contested status already records; and the original authors' reply to two letters (Fung et al., 2008; Mariani, 2008) concedes that the cohort's flow figure was wrong, confirms the classification already rated at critical risk of bias (without the admissions given a beta-blocker after their infarction, its crude estimate is 0.31, 0.08 to 1.21, editors' calculation) and states that blood pressure after the drug was not consistently recorded. None of these changes the evidence base, so the certainty (very low) and the status (contested) are unchanged. Companion paper of 12 November, read in full: Espana Schmidt et al. (2015; card sc_espana_schmidt_2015, first pass, ROBINS-I serious), the cohort that Lo et al. and Shin et al. pooled and Pham et al. did not, compared 26 patients given one beta-blocker dose in the emergency department with 32 selected comparison patients (of 378 admitted) and found no deaths or recorded cardiac complications in either group, no blood-pressure or heart-rate difference, and troponin results with no stated threshold that it does not call infarctions; the two reviews entered those results as infarctions (Lo et al.: the first window, 20.5% of the weight) or as infarction or necrosis summed over three windows (Shin et al.: 23.2% of the weight, the most of any cohort), and without them no pooled estimate becomes significant and the remaining cohorts still agree (editors' calculations). It adds 58 patients without an event to evidence already counted in two of the reviews, so neither the evidence base nor the rating changes: certainty very low and status contested, unchanged. Not read: the two cohorts that only Shin et al. pooled, the erratum to Dattilo et al. that the reply announces, and a letter published on Rangel et al. (2010).

debate.question: Does a beta-blocker given in hospital to someone with chest pain after cocaine narrow the heart's arteries further and make heart attacks or deaths more likely, as a 1990 laboratory study and the 2008 American Heart Association statement suggest (Lange et al., 1990; McCord et al., 2008), or not, as hospital records have been read to show (Lo et al., 2019; Pham et al., 2018; Shin et al., 2019)?
debate.evidence_yes: In the one randomized laboratory study, propranolol infused into the left coronary artery of 10 catheterization patients 15 minutes after intranasal cocaine was followed by a further fall in coronary blood flow (120 to 100 mL/min, P = 0.050 against the post-cocaine value) and a further rise in resistance (P = 0.074), in the same direction in all 10, changes not seen in 5 patients given a saline infusion after cocaine or in 5 given propranolol without cocaine; 5 of the 10 had an artery segment narrow by more than 10%, and one had a complete coronary occlusion with ischaemic symptoms and ST-segment elevation (Lange et al., 1990). The explanation offered, that blocking beta receptors leaves cocaine's stimulation of alpha receptors in the arteries unopposed, underlies the American Heart Association's 2008 Class III recommendation to avoid beta-blockers in the acute setting, which also cites animal experiments in which beta-blockers decreased coronary blood flow and increased seizures and deaths, and reports, second-hand, that the short-acting beta-1 blocker esmolol raised blood pressure significantly in up to 25% of patients (McCord et al., 2008). In hospital records, patients already taking a beta-blocker when they arrived had a raised troponin more often (14 of 100, against 4.4% of the others), and a later troponin rise was reported more often when a beta-blocker was continued or started in hospital (23.3% against 10.7%) (Mohamad et al., 2008); in another cohort troponin rose in 13.6% of treated patients against 9.3% (Ibrahim et al., 2013); and the pooled in-hospital estimates for infarction lean towards harm (odds ratio 1.36, upper limit 2.74, Pham et al., 2018; relative risk 1.24, upper limit 2.06, Shin et al., 2019), Shin et al.'s a little further once its largest row, troponin results from a cohort that counted no infarctions, is left out (1.30, upper limit 2.57, editors' calculation; Espana Schmidt et al., 2015; Shin et al., 2019). In the cohort with an analysis by drug type, the estimates were 1.83 for beta-1-selective drugs and 0.90 for drugs that also block alpha receptors, the pattern the unopposed-alpha explanation predicts, though the difference was not tested (Fanari et al., 2014). In an editorial printed with the Bronx cohort, an emergency physician of the New York City Poison Center argued that the catheterization and animal studies justified the caution, that little benefit is possible when infarction occurs in 5% to 6% of these patients and in-hospital deaths approach zero, and that, although cases of harm are rarely reported, the evidence still speaks against beta-blockers in this setting and a trial would be premature and dangerous (Hoffman, 2008).
debate.evidence_no: No study has measured a clinical outcome of beta-blockers after cocaine in a randomized comparison, and apart from one unadjusted comparison (Mohamad et al., 2008) no cohort found a significant increase in infarction or death with a beta-blocker given in hospital. Beta-blockers were often given despite the guidance (to 44% of 376 patients with cocaine-positive chest pain in 2000–2007), and the patients who received one, although older and with more heart disease, did not have detectably more in-hospital infarction, stroke, arrhythmia or death after adjustment for a propensity score (odds ratio 1.37, 0.64 to 2.93); deaths were 3% against 6% (Fanari et al., 2014). In another cohort, troponin in the infarction range was found in 10% of patients with and without a beta-blocker in the emergency department, death over a median 972 days, the primary outcome, was not associated with it (hazard ratio 0.97, 0.53 to 1.79), and systolic blood pressure fell after the beta-blocker (median −8 mm Hg) rather than rising, as unopposed alpha stimulation would predict, though it had started higher (Rangel et al., 2010). One cohort reported fewer infarctions after a beta-blocker (2 of 33 against 72 of 277) (Dattilo et al., 2008). In another, none of 26 patients given one dose of a beta-blocker in the emergency department while their chest pain continued, and none of 32 comparison patients, died or had a recorded cardiac complication, and blood pressure and heart rate were no higher than in the comparison group at any time up to 6 hours, which the authors read as no sign of unopposed alpha stimulation (Espana Schmidt et al., 2015). Pooling the cohorts gave no significant difference in infarction or death in three reviews (Lo et al., 2019; Pham et al., 2018; Shin et al., 2019), including one that left out Mohamad et al.'s cohort (risk ratio for infarction 1.08, 0.61 to 1.91; Lo et al., 2019); their authors conclude that the guidelines should be reconsidered (Pham et al., 2018, one of whose authors also wrote the 2008 statement), that the suggested ill effects of beta-blockers are not borne out by existing evidence (Lo et al., 2019) and that beta-blockers may not be as harmful as believed (Shin et al., 2019). The laboratory case for harm is narrow: 19 people received a blocker after cocaine in the two studies, none with a history of cocaine use; propranolol went directly into a coronary artery at one dose; the rise in resistance did not reach the authors' own threshold against the post-cocaine value (P = 0.074), the average artery diameters did not change, the randomized comparison was not tested, and the authors could not exclude a fall in the heart's contractility as the reason flow fell (Lange et al., 1990). Labetalol, which also blocks alpha receptors, did not narrow the arteries further in 9 patients and lowered blood pressure (Boehrer et al., 1993). The AHA statement grades its recommendation Level of Evidence C and marks no clinical trial or observational study behind it (McCord et al., 2008). In a second editorial printed with the Bronx cohort, two physicians argued that the caution rests on uncontrolled observations, beginning with a 1985 report of one patient whose blood pressure rose after propranolol, on surrogate end points and on animal models; that beta-blockers are of established benefit in other conditions with high catecholamine levels, such as heart failure; and that they should not be withheld from patients with an acute coronary syndrome and a positive urine test who are not acutely intoxicated, while for acute intoxication research, not opinion, should decide (Freeman & Feldman, 2008).
debate.neither_can_show: The laboratory studies measured artery size, blood flow and resistance for minutes after one moderate intranasal dose in cardiac patients with no history of cocaine use (Lange et al., 1990; Boehrer et al., 1993), so they cannot show what happens to people who use cocaine, at the amounts they use, when a beta-blocker is given by vein or by mouth, or whether any heart attack or death follows. The hospital cohorts cannot show it either: doctors chose whom to treat, and the treated patients were older, had more heart disease and received more aspirin, nitrates and other heart drugs (Fanari et al., 2014), while the least stable patients may not have been treated (vasopressors in 1% against 7%; Rangel et al., 2010); the drug was counted over windows that do not match the outcomes, from beta-blockers already taken before arrival (Mohamad et al., 2008) to infarctions counted only after the drug in the treated group but from admission in the others (Dattilo et al., 2008), as its authors confirmed in reply to a letter while conceding that their flow figure was wrong (Fung et al., 2008), and a drug given at unknown times (Ibrahim et al., 2013); urine screens stay positive for 2 to 3 days, so whether cocaine was still active is unknown (Fanari et al., 2014; Pham et al., 2018), a point both editorials printed with the Bronx cohort make (Freeman & Feldman, 2008; Hoffman, 2008); infarction was defined by troponin thresholds from 0.02 to 1.5 ng/mL (Shin et al., 2019); the drugs mixed beta-1-selective agents with agents that also block alpha receptors; and the intervals include both appreciable harm and appreciable benefit. By the authors' own account, in reply to a letter, the Bronx records did not consistently hold blood pressure after the drug, so they cannot show whether it rose, as unopposed alpha stimulation would predict (Mariani, 2008). The Metropolitan Hospital cohort compared 26 treated patients with 32 chosen in a way not described, from admissions defined by a final diagnosis of cocaine-induced chest pain, so its lack of events cannot exclude a risk of up to 13.2% with a beta-blocker (editors' calculation), and its troponin results, with no threshold given, cannot show infarction (Espana Schmidt et al., 2015). All three meta-analyses pooled unadjusted counts from overlapping cohorts, with several entries that do not match the primary papers, among them one cohort's long-term deaths pooled as in-hospital deaths and another's troponin results pooled as infarctions, in one review summed over three time windows (Lo et al., 2019; Pham et al., 2018; Shin et al., 2019).
debate.editors_reading: The editors' reading: that cocaine narrows the coronary arteries and lowers coronary blood flow in the minutes after use is shown in a randomized, placebo-controlled laboratory study, though in a small, selected group (people with no history of cocaine use, given one moderate dose) (Lange et al., 1990). Whether a beta-blocker given in hospital makes outcomes worse is not known, and certainty is very low. A plausible mechanism, seen in 10 people given propranolol into a coronary artery (Lange et al., 1990), points to harm; hospital records of about 2,000 patients neither show nor exclude harm (Shin et al., 2019), a third pooling of largely the same cohorts adds no independent evidence (Lo et al., 2019), a sixth cohort, already inside two of the reviews, adds 58 patients without a death or recorded complication, whose troponin results those reviews counted as infarctions (Espana Schmidt et al., 2015), and the single cohorts disagree only where their designs are most biased (Dattilo et al., 2008; Mohamad et al., 2008). The American Heart Association's Class III recommendation is expert consensus resting on the laboratory studies, not on outcomes in patients (McCord et al., 2008); the meta-analyses' suggestion that beta-blockers may be safe rests on unadjusted, confounded and partly misentered counts from the same cohorts (Lo et al., 2019; Pham et al., 2018; Shin et al., 2019). The evidence read settles neither the recommendation nor its reversal.
debate.what_would_settle_it: A randomized trial in people who come to hospital with chest pain after recent, confirmed cocaine use, comparing an intravenous beta-blocker (beta-1-selective and combined alpha-beta blockers separately) with the treatments the 2008 statement grades Class I (benzodiazepines and nitroglycerin; McCord et al., 2008), with blinded assessment of infarction, arrhythmia and death and enough events to exclude a meaningful difference; the cohorts' authors call for such a trial (Dattilo et al., 2008; Rangel et al., 2010; Fanari et al., 2014), and none had been reported by June 2018 (Shin et al., 2019), nor any trial with clinical outcomes by July 2018 (Lo et al., 2019). Short of that, an individual-patient analysis of the existing cohorts with a common starting point for treated and untreated patients, every eligible patient analysed rather than a selected comparison group (Espana Schmidt et al., 2015), one troponin definition, adjusted estimates, separation by drug type and by when the drug was given, and in-hospital and long-term deaths kept apart, which one review pooled together (Lo et al., 2019).

statement: In 50 US one-dollar bills in general circulation, 10 each from four US cities (Baltimore, Chicago, Denver and Honolulu) and San Juan, Puerto Rico, obtained in everyday purchases on dates not stated before November 2000 and tested in a US federal laboratory by gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (Jenkins, 2001), 46 carried detectable cocaine (92%; editors' Wilson 95% interval 81% to 97%): every bill from four of the places and 6 of the 10 from Chicago. The amounts were small and very uneven: on the 46 bills with cocaine the median was 1.37 µg (micrograms, millionths of a gram) and 18 carried less than 1 µg, while the printed mean of 28.75 µg is pulled up by two bills, one with 233.55 µg and one with 922.72 µg, the latter holding about 70% of all the cocaine measured (editors' recomputation from the paper's table, which also shows that the printed mean and median refer to the 46 bills with cocaine only). A few bills carried other drugs: heroin 7, 6-acetylmorphine and morphine 3, methamphetamine 3, amphetamine 1, PCP 2 and codeine none; the methamphetamine amounts (0.55 µg, 0.60 µg and under 1 µg) appear to lie below the method's lowest calibration point (editors' calculation), so they are not precise values. No new or uncirculated bills were tested as blanks, recovery of drug from paper was not checked and the bills were a convenience collection, so the study describes these 50 bills, not money in general, in other countries or today. It measured nothing in people: the author's judgement that handling such bills is unlikely to make a urine drug test positive rests on one cited earlier experiment in which one person handled two bills dipped in coca paste, whose urine showed the cocaine metabolite benzoylecgonine at 72, 36 and 24 ng/ml between 12.5 and 21 hours, below the 300 ng/ml cut-off used, and the judgement is extended to drugs that experiment did not test. The paper has no funding statement; the analyses were done at the US National Institute on Drug Abuse. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
plain: Do most US dollar bills carry traces of cocaine? In one study, 46 of 50 one-dollar bills collected in everyday purchases in four US cities and San Juan, Puerto Rico, by 2000 carried cocaine. The typical bill held a little over a millionth of a gram, and one Honolulu bill held about 7 in 10 of all the cocaine found, so the average makes a typical bill look more contaminated than it was. A few bills also carried heroin, methamphetamine or PCP. No unused bills were tested for comparison, and money elsewhere or today may differ. Nobody was drug-tested in this study: the author's view that handling such bills is unlikely to make a urine drug test positive rests on an earlier test of one person.
population: 50 US$1 bills in general circulation, 10 each from Baltimore, Chicago, Denver, Honolulu and San Juan (Puerto Rico), obtained in everyday purchases on dates not stated before November 2000
exposure: Circulation as everyday money (the bills, not people, were studied)
comparator: None: no new or uncirculated bills were analysed, the solvent alone was the drug-free control, and the places are compared descriptively
outcome: Detectable cocaine on each bill and its amount in micrograms (µg) per bill; also heroin, 6-acetylmorphine, morphine, codeine, methamphetamine, amphetamine and PCP
magnitude: Jenkins (2001): cocaine on 46 of 50 bills (92%; editors' Wilson 95% interval 81.2% to 96.8%); 10 of 10 in Baltimore, Denver, Honolulu and San Juan, 6 of 10 in Chicago. Bills with cocaine: median 1.37 µg, mean 28.75 µg with a spread of 139.07 (the sample standard deviation of the 46, editors' recomputation), range 0.01–922.72 µg; 18 of 46 below 1 µg and 2 above 100 µg (233.55 and 922.72 µg); over all 50 bills, counting undetected as zero, mean 26.45 µg and median 1.24 µg (editors'); the 922.72 µg bill held 69.8% of the 1,322.32 µg measured in all, and the other 45 bills with cocaine averaged 8.88 µg (editors'). Heroin 7 of 50 (0.03–168.50 µg); 6-acetylmorphine and morphine 3; methamphetamine 3 (0.55, 0.60 and under 1 µg, below the lowest calibrator by the editors' calculation); amphetamine 1 (0.85 µg); PCP 2 (0.78 and 1.87 µg); codeine 0. Cited experiment (ElSohly, as cited): 1 person; urine benzoylecgonine negative to 8.5 h, 72, 36 and 24 ng/ml at 12.5, 18 and 21 h, then negative; negative at a 300 ng/ml cut-off.

evidence.locator: Title block and Abstract (p. 189); 2.2 Collection of dollar bills and 2.3 Extraction (p. 190); Discussion, 3rd paragraph (begins on p. 191, continued on p. 192)
evidence.extracted: Single author from a county coroner's office in Cleveland, Ohio; received 3 November 2000, revised 22 December 2000, accepted 8 January 2001; the dates on which the bills were collected are not stated. US$1 bills in general circulation were collected, described as randomly, from four US cities (Baltimore, Chicago, Denver and Honolulu) and San Juan, Puerto Rico, 10 from each; the Discussion says they were obtained in day-to-day transactions in stores, restaurants and admission fees to public sites, and no sampling procedure is described. On collection the bills were put in plastic storage bags (whether singly is not stated) and kept at room temperature until analysis in the intramural research programme of the US National Institute on Drug Abuse in Baltimore. Each bill was placed separately in a tube with 5 ml of acetonitrile and vortexed four times for 30 s over 2 h, and 1 ml of extract was taken for each assay; acetonitrile alone served as the drug-free control, and no new or uncirculated bills were analysed.

evidence.locator: 2.4 Analysis, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (p. 190); 3.3 Denver and 3.4 Honolulu (p. 191)
evidence.extracted: Cocaine, PCP and codeine were measured against an eight-point calibration run in duplicate (cocaine 3.1–1000 ng/ml, codeine 2.5–500, PCP 1.25–250) and heroin, 6-acetylmorphine and morphine against a six-point calibration (2.5–50 ng/ml), in both cases with samples diluted when necessary to fall within the range and detection limits of about 1.0 ng/ml; methamphetamine and amphetamine were measured against a four-point calibration of 500–5000 ng/ml, with a limit of detection and quantitation of about 100 ng/ml and no dilution mentioned. The paper does not say how concentrations in the extract were converted to amounts per bill, and no recovery of drug from paper is reported. Methamphetamine was reported at 0.55 and 0.60 µg (Denver) and under 1 µg (Honolulu), amphetamine at 0.85 µg. Editors' calculation, assuming amounts were computed from the 5 ml extract: 0.55, 0.60 and 0.85 µg correspond to about 110, 120 and 170 ng/ml, below the lowest calibration point (500 ng/ml) and just above the stated limit, so these amounts are extrapolated and should not be read as precise values; under the same assumption the smallest cocaine amount (0.01 µg, Baltimore bill 6) corresponds to about 2 ng/ml, below the lowest cocaine calibrator (3.1 ng/ml) and above its detection limit.

evidence.locator: Discussion, 5th paragraph
evidence.extracted: The author cites one earlier experiment (ElSohly, as cited): two US$1 bills were immersed in powdered coca paste, the loose powder was shaken off, and the bills were given to one person, who handled them several times through the day without washing the hands; urine collected up to 8.5 h after first handling was negative for the cocaine metabolite benzoylecgonine by immunoassay, samples at 12.5, 18 and 21 h were positive at 72, 36 and 24 ng/ml (measured semiquantitatively), later samples were negative, and at a 300 ng/ml cut-off the person was negative. On this basis the author judges it unlikely that cocaine or the other drugs found in this study could pass to people handling money in amounts that would make a urine test positive. This study tested no people, and the cited experiment used coca paste only.

evidence.extracted: Background given in the Introduction, not studied here: US bills are thought to be contaminated mainly by people who roll them up to take cocaine, with drug deals contributing and bank counting machines transferring small amounts to other bills; an earlier study is cited for amounts of 0 to 1327 µg per bill on randomly collected bills. In the Discussion the author compares earlier reports, as cited: cocaine on 131 of 135 bills of US$1 to US$100 from banks in 12 US cities, averaging 7.3 µg per bill (Hearn); typically under 1 ng per Canadian banknote from the Bank of Canada, and averages of 2.7 to 1069 ng per note on notes seized in drug investigations (Hudson); and an upper limit of 13 ng per bill for the general background, with over 95% of bills below it, on US bills from financial institutions (Jourdan and Donnelly). The author says the microgram amounts found here disagree with the nanogram findings of Hudson and of Jourdan and Donnelly and, for the latter, suggests that the different sources of the bills (financial institutions there, everyday transactions here) may partly explain the difference. The summary says microgram amounts of drug may be present on bills in general circulation and that contamination of currency other than US and Canadian dollars had not been reported.

risk_of_bias.note: Card sc_jenkins_2001 (editors' checklist for laboratory analyses of samples, first pass, some concerns overall): a convenience collection of bills called random without a procedure, on unstated dates, kept in plastic bags whose sharing is not stated; no new or uncirculated bills carried through as blanks, only a solvent blank, so contamination during collection, storage or laboratory handling cannot be excluded for the low-level results, which make up much of the 92%; no recovery from paper and no stated conversion from extract concentration to amount per bill. The four Chicago bills without cocaine show that the method could return negatives.

inconsistency.note: One study; the earlier studies it cites (cocaine on most bills in one, nanogram levels in two others) are second-hand and not rated.

indirectness.note: 50 US one-dollar bills from four US cities and San Juan, collected by 2000; not other denominations, other countries' money or money today, and nothing was measured in people (drug tests) or dogs.

imprecision.note: 46 of 50 (editors' Wilson 95% interval 81% to 97%) answers 'most' for this collection even at its lower limit; the amounts are summarized by the median because two bills dominate the mean; the methamphetamine amounts, which are imprecise, are not part of the main finding.

grade.reasoning: A laboratory description of objects (banknotes), rated as a description of the bills sampled, starts low; rated down one level for risk of bias (convenience collection, no blank bills, no recovery from paper) and one for indirectness (50 one-dollar bills from five places in the US and Puerto Rico, collected by 2000), it is very low, the floor. Status single study: the earlier studies the author cites (cocaine on 131 of 135 bills from banks; nanogram levels on Canadian notes and on US bills from financial institutions) are summarized in the paper and not read here, so they are not counted. Rated as worded: the share of these bills with detectable cocaine and the amounts on them. The paper's judgement that handling money is unlikely to produce a positive urine drug test is reported as the author's, with its basis (one person in a cited experiment), and is not rated, because this study tested no people; whether handling money can make a drug test positive would be a separate answer from studies of people.
